word.notes: A first person plural object pronoun “us” attested only in the prepositional phrase “on us” in the , developing though the various drafts as nēnum >> nēnu >> nēnud (SD/247, 312). Most authors identify the element nê as the pronoun (/20, , /14), which seems likely since the prepositional element is probably -num/nu/nud related to Q. “under”. It is not clear whether this pronoun can also be used as a subject pronoun “we”, or if it must always be an object “us”.

Only nouns for inanimate objects may be neuter. Words for animals (but perhaps not plants) and for people whose gender is unspecified are declined as instead of neuters (SD/426).

Neuter nouns do not end in the long vowels -ê, -î, -ô, -û, and do not have a long î or û in their final syllable (SD/427), though monosyllables seem to be an exception to the second rule: see “breath” and “shout” (SD/426). These vowels are considered markers of femininity or masculinity (SD/435), and are therefore not applicable to neuter (or common) nouns. There is one attested exception to this rule, “Elvish” (SD/414), but the in this case seems to be a suffix. Most neuter nouns have a short vowel in their last syllable (that is, they are a ). If they have a long vowel in the last syllable, it is usually â, such as “road” or “chasm”. In the case of a final long vowel, it must be -â, such as “hand”.
The masculine personification of “the moon” (SD/426), perhaps the Adûnaic name for Q. .

A noun translated as “moon” and fully declined as an example of a Strong II noun (SD/431). It appears with both a short and long final -u, but Tolkien indicated that the form with long û is actually the personified form “Man in the Moon” (SD/426), perhaps the Adûnaic name of . Tolkien also listed the “later forms Nil, Njūl” (SD/306), one of which may be the Westron word for “moon”, most likely Wes. . Andreas Moehn suggested (/NUL) that this noun may be related to nûlo/nûlu/nâlu, but given the evil connotations of these words (SD/306) and the different stem vowels, this seems unlikely to me.
A Primitive Adûnaic root glossed “shine” (SD/416), apparently the basis for “Elf”.

A noun translated “Elf” (WJ/419) and fully declined as an example of a Strong I noun (SD/436). In one place, its plural Nimrî was translated “Shining Ones” (SD/358), which indicates was probably derived from the Primitive Adûnaic root √.

Conceptual Development: In its earliest appearances from the 1940s, this noun had the plural form Nimrî (SD/358, 388) as opposed to later plural Nimîr (SD/388, 436), which could indicate either an earlier singular form Nimri or a variant syntax for formation. The word also appears in Tolkien’s Quendi and Eldar essay from 1959-60 (WJ/386), indicating that this word survived in Tolkien’s later conception of Adûnaic.
The Adûnaic word for the Elvish language (SD/414), most likely a combination of the word “Elf” (evidently with the Adûnaic ) and a suffix meaning “language”, perhaps .

The Adûnaic name for Q. “Elf-friend”, almost certainly with the same meaning (SD/247). The first element is the form of “Elf” and the second element is an for “*to love” (SD/389).

Conceptual Development: The first Adûnaic version of this name, Nimruzân, shares the same suffix as the first Adûnaic version of his father’s Adûnaic name .

A noun meaning “Elf-friend”, attested only in the () plural form Nimruzîrim (PM/151). It is identical to the Adûnaic name of Q. , which had the same meaning.

Conceptual Development: An earlier name for the faithful Númenóreans was (SD/347).

An early name of the Númenóreans who remained faithful to the Valar, later called the “Elf-friends”: Ad. Nimruzîrim, Q. . It is not clear what language this word belongs to, but it may contain the word Adûnaic word for the Valar: .

A noun translated “girl” and fully declined as an example of a feminine Strong I noun (SD/430). It is also used as an example of feminine nouns that use the suffix -i in their inflection as opposed to the usual -u: nithli (SD/431). Though not explicitly stated, nithli is also an example of the variant objective-with-syncope syntax discussed on SD/435. Carl Hostetter and Patrick Wynne suggested (/21) it may be related to the Elvish root √ “young”.

A verb attested only as an in the names “Star-kindler” and “kindler of a (particular) star” (SD/428). Thorsten Renk suggested (/32) the base verb is nitir-, and this seems to me to be the likeliest possibility. Andreas Moehn instead suggested (/NIT’Y) that the verb stem may be nit-, and that the -îr is some kind of feminine agental suffix.

The Adûnaic “normal case” is simply the default form with no special inflections. In most circumstances, the noun appears in the normal case, in all situation except where the or cases would be used. The possibilities are discussed on SD/428-9.

1) As the direct object of a verb:

  • Bârim yurahtam dâira “The Lords broke the Earth” (SD/247) = Bârim (subjective plural) + yurahtam (verb) + (normal).

2) As the object of preposition (which are suffixal in Adûnaic):

  • akhâsada “into the chasm” (SD/247) = (normal) + (prepositional suffix).

3) Before another noun in an adjectival or possessive relationship:

  • agannâlu “death shadow” (SD/247) = (normal) + .

4) As a predicate in a copula (whose subject would be in the subjective case):

  • Ar-Pharazônun kathuphazgân “Ar-Pharazôn is a conqueror” (SD/429) = Ar-Pharazônun (subjective) + (normal)

5) The subject of a sentence was usually in the subjective case, but could be in the normal case if the verb was inflected with the proper pronominal prefix. Compare:

  • bârun kallaba “the lord fell” (SD/429) = bârun (subjective) + kallaba (verb without pronoun)
  • bâr ukallaba “the lord fell” (SD/429) = (normal) + ukallaba (verb with pronoun)

The subjective formation puts more emphasis on the subject. This is especially true if it was combined with a verb using a pronominal prefix:

  • bârun ukallaba “it was the lord who fell” (SD/429) = bârun (subjective) + ukallaba (verb with pronoun)

Adûnaic had three formal noun cases (SD/428):

  • The : The default case used most of the time.
  • The case: Used (with some exceptions) for the subject of a sentence.
  • The case: Used only in compounds, for the object of a verbal phrase.

The normal and subjective cases could be declined for all numbers (singular, dual and plural), but the objective case could only be used in the singular.

In combination with classification by , Adûnaic nouns can be classified as either strong-nouns or weak-nouns (SD/425). Strong nouns modify the vowel of their last syllable when declined into most , while weak nouns add some sort of suffix (SD/430). Generally speaking, monosyllabic nouns and nouns with a long vowel or diphthong in their last syllable are classified as weak (SD/431), while polysyllabic nouns with a short vowel in their last syllable are strong.

In addition to the strong and weak classification, Adûnaic noun declensions differ for nouns ending in a consonant (Class I) versus those ending in a vowel (Class II). For Class I nouns, there is at most one final consonant, since clusters are not allowed as in Adûnaic. In combination with the strong and weak classifications, this gives us four groups:

Classes of Adûnaic Nouns
Strong IEnding in a single consonant preceded by a short vowel✧ SD/430, 436-7
Strong IIEnding in a short vowel✧ SD/431, 437
Weak IEnding in a single consonant preceded by a long vowel or diphthong✧ SD/431-2, 437-8
Weak IIEnding in a long vowel or diphthong✧ SD/438

Tolkien labeled the weak classes Weak (a) and Weak (b) (SD/437-8), but the discussion here uses Weak I and Weak II for consistency with the Strong class names. Also remember that monosyllables are always weak, though all attested Adûnaic monosyllables have a long vowel or diphthong making them weak in any case.

There is a small group of nouns (Strong Ib and Strong IIb) that used strong declensions despite having a long vowel in their last syllable (SD/437). These declensions are archaic, however, and the weak declensions can be used for such nouns by the time of Classical Adûnaic.

Noun declensions also vary depending on the of the noun. These three factors combine to determine how a noun is declined: gender, strong versus weak, class I versus class II.

Like English, Adûnaic has separate forms for singular and plural nouns, and like Quenya it has an additional form used for pairs of nouns: the dual (SD/427). Markers for these numbers are:
  • Singular: the unmodified form of the noun.
  • Plural: uses the plural inflection .
  • Dual: uses the dual suffix .

Adûnaic nouns end in either a vowel or a single consonant, since clusters were not allowed as in Adûnaic (SD/426). In cases where the noun was originally produced by a suffix, it is limited to the final consonants used in . In cases where the noun is “basic”, that is derived directly from a primitive biconsonantal- or such as PUH or PHARAZ, it can end in any consonant.

Tolkien indicated that such basic noun forms are uncommon except in , though they are quite common in neuters (SD/426). Basic nouns are particularly rare for , the only commonly-used example being “girl” (SD/426-7). Such basic nouns are generally the only way an Adûnaic noun can end in a consonant without suffixion.

Primitive Adûnaic nouns always had at least two consonants (SD/416). Classical Adûnaic nouns that seem to be exceptions to this rule have all undergone some kind of consonant loss from its primitive form, either because a primitive consonant vanished, as with “God” < √ (SD/432), or because a primitive consonant became a vowel, as with “hand” < ✶ and “crow” < khau < ✶ (SD/426).

A preposition attested only in the phrase “on us” in the , changing through the drafts as nēnum >> nēnu >> nēnud (SD/247, 312). Most authors identify -nud as the prepositional element (/20, , /14), perhaps related to Q. “under”. If so, it may be a derivative of the Elvish roots √ “under” or √ “down”, with a semantic shift to the meaning “on”.

We only know two Adûnaic numbers: “two” (SD/428) and “seven” (SD/247). The Adûnaic number for “one” might be *ir, derived from the root √ “one, alone”; we do know that the number “one” was the only number not considered a noun (SD/428). All other numbers are considered nouns and follow the noun they modify: gimlî hazad “seven stars” (SD/428). Formally, the number is in a genitive relationship with the noun: “seven of ships”. Most nouns that precede a number are inflected into the plural, but nouns that precede the number two are left in the singular: nârdu satta “two soldier[s]” (SD/428).

A noun translated “fool” and fully declined as an example of a Weak I noun (SD/437-8). It was later written in the form nîph (SD/426), but since all the attested declensions are based on nûph, the entry here uses the earlier form.

The word nûph is a common-noun but it has some example inflections with masculine and feminine suffixes: nûphun (masculine subjective), nûphin (feminine subjective), nûphi (feminine objective). This seems to be another way that an individual’s gender be indicated (“male fool”, “female fool”) instead of using explicit masucline and feminine suffixes like or .

A noun translated “parent” (SD/434). It also appears in the dual form nuphrât “father and mother”, but this dual form is peculiar. As a weak II noun, the dual form ought to be *nuphârat, as for example “road” → batânat “pair of roads” (SD/431). Its dual form seems instead to undergo the Adûnaic (vowel loss), which happens nowhere else with a long vowel. There is no obvious explanation for this irregular formation.

A prepositional suffix translated “from” (SD/429). In a few places, the suffix appears with the v (pronounced ) between it and a preceding u-vowel (SD/247, 249). It is likely related to the Quenya genitive inflection Q. .

Conceptual Development: At an earlier conceptual stage, this suffix was a grammatical inflection, the (SD/438).
The suffix used for the case, with a plural form -ōm (SD/438). In a later conceptual stage, it became the ordinary prepositional suffix .

A prepositional element only attested in the late (1968) word “fore-cutting” (PM/376), referring to the wake before a boat, so perhaps meaning “*before”. It appears only as a suffix, but in the earlier Adûnaic grammar of Lowdham’s Report from the 1940s, Adûnaic are used as suffixes (SD/435). This preposition also differs from the earlier phonetic rules of Lowdham’s Report, which allow only long in Adûnaic words. If this preposition were used in the grammatical and phonetic context of Lowdham’s Report (Middle Adûnaic), it might be the suffix *-ôb. See the entry on for further discussion.

The objective case is formed with the objective inflection and is used only in the initial elements of some compounds (SD/429-30).

Objective Usage

Despite its name, the objective case is not used for the direct object of a verb. Such direct objects are left in the normal case (SD/428):

  • Bârim yurahtam dâira “The Lords broke the Earth” (SD/247).

The objective case is only used for the initial elements of compounds, when the element is the object of a second verbal element (SD/429). It appears mainly in Adûnaic names:

  • Balkumagân “Shipwright, *Ship-builder” (PM/151).
  • Azrubêl “Sea-lover” (PM/373, SD/305, 429).

The objective is often combined with a verb used in an , in which case it is the object of that verb (SD/429):

  • Azrubêl “Sea-lover” = (objective) + “love” (agental) (PM/373, SD/427).
  • izindu-bêth “truth-sayer” = (objective) + bêth (?) “say” (agental) (SD/427).

Other times the objective is used with a noun that is perceived to have a verbal function (SD/429):

  • Balkumagân “Shipwright” = “boat” (objective) + “wright, *builder” = builder of boats (PM/151).
  • Minul-târik “Pillar of Heaven” = “heaven” (objective) + “pillar, that which supports” = that which supports heaven (SD/429).

When nouns are combined without using the objective, the initial noun generally functions as an adjectival or possessive modifier of the second (SD/429):

  • “heavenly pillar” = a pillar composed of heavenly material, such as clouds (SD/429).
  • “sea-lands” = lands made of the sea (SD/429).

The objective form is only used for singular nouns. When plural nouns (or ) are in the same position, they are always considered to be in an object-relationship and therefore do not need to be declined into the objective (SD/429):

  • Gimilnitîr “Star-kindler” = “all stars” (objective) + “kindle” (agental) = kindler of all the stars (SD/428).

Where a plural noun needs to be in an adjectival or possessive relationship with another noun, it must be used in conjunction with the genitival prefix (SD/429).

  • “King of the Númenóreans” = “king” + “of” + Adûnâi “Númenóreans” (plural) (SD/429).

Note the change in word order, as such phrases appear after the noun, as opposed to the objective or adjectival formations which appear before.

Objective Formation

The objective is formed with the objective inflection (SD/430). This inflection changes the last vowel of a (those with a short vowel in the last syllable) and is added as a suffix to a (those with a long vowel or diphthong in the last syllable).

  • Strong: “pool” → khibul (objective, SD/430).
  • Strong: “dog” → rabu (objective, SD/437).
  • Weak: “road” → batânu (objective, SD/431).
  • Weak: “spirit” → manô (objective, SD/438).

In the last example, the suffix -u is absorbed by the final vowel -ô according to the standard Adûnaic rules for . The same would happen with a final vowel -û, so that the normal and objective forms would be identical in these cases. Masculine nouns often end in these two vowels, and such nouns do not have distinct objective forms.

Owing to the association of the vowel u with the masculine gender (SD/427), the objective forms of often use the vowel i in the objective case by the time of Classical Adûnaic (SD/432). For the numerous feminine nouns ending in -ê and -î, this variant objective suffix is absorbed by the final vowel so that (like masculine nouns) their normal and objective forms are the same.

  • “baby girl” → mîthi (feminine objective) vs. older †mîthu (SD/438).
  • “nurse” → zôrî (feminine objective suffix absorbed) vs. older †zôrîyu (SD/438).
  • “sweetheart” → izrê (feminine objective suffix absorbed) vs. older †izrâyu (SD/438).

Objective With Syncope (Strong I nouns)

Nouns ending in a consonant preceded by a short vowel (Strong I nouns) often use a variant form of the objective with the Adûnaic and the objective inflection added as a suffixal -u (SD/435). Originally, such Strong I nouns with the short vowel u would have identical normal and subjective forms.

  • “ear” → huzun (objective, SD/430) with the last vowel “changed” to u

To better distinguish the normal and objective forms, such nouns could have an alternate objective inflection that suppresses the last vowel and adds the suffix -u. This followed the normal pattern for the Adûnaic syncope, and the discussion here use the term “objective with syncope” to refer to this formation.

  • “ear” → huznu (objective with syncope, SD/430).

Later, this formation spread to nouns that had the other short vowels as well. In the case of feminine nouns, the suffixal addition could be -i instead of -u, as noted above.

  • “ship” → balku (objective with syncope, PM/151).
  • “girl” → nithli (feminine objective with syncope, SD/431).

Both the “objective with syncope” and “feminine i-suffix” rules for the objective were optional, sometimes seen and sometimes not. Where the Adûnaic was prohibited (such as for nouns with two different vowels), the objective with syncope was probably prohibited as well.

  • “heaven” → minul (objective, SD/429).

Archaic and Irregular Objective Forms

There are several objective forms that do not comply with the rules above, but Tolkien indicated that most of these formations were archaic.

Archaic Strong Objectives: Some weak-nouns could have a strong objective declension, replacing their last vowel with u instead of adding the -u as a suffix. This was because either (a) the noun was originally a strong noun, later becoming weak when its final vowel was lengthened or (b) it belonged to the small class of nouns (Strong Ib and Strong IIb) that were strong despite having a long vowel in the final syllable:

  • †zini “female” → †zinu (archaic strong objective) vs. newer normal and objective forms (SD/437).
  • “prince” → †phazûn (archaic strong objective) vs. newer objective form phazânu (SD/437).

Archaic Objectives with Glide Consonants: Archaically, ending in -ê or -î would using the glide consonant y before the objective suffix -u. In the case of -ê, this long vowel would decompose into -ây (or perhaps -ay), as discussed in the section on “Archaic Glide Consonants with -ê and -ô” in the entry on the :

  • “nurse” → †zôrîyu (archaic objective with glide) vs. newer form zôrî (feminine objective with suffix absorbed, SD/438).
  • “sweetheart” → †izrâyu (archaic objective with glide) vs. newer form izrê (feminine objective with suffix absorbed, SD/438).

Archaic Feminine Objectives with -u: All of the archaic objectives of feminine nouns used the objective -u instead of the variant feminine suffix -i discussed above. This -u would not be absorbed by final feminine vowels. It is not clear whether the u-suffix has been entirely replaced by the i-suffix by the time of Classical Adûnaic, or whether u could still be used with some feminine nouns.

Adjectives in the Objective Case: There are a couple of examples of adjectives declined into the objective case as part of compounds:

  • “true-sayer, prophet” contains “straight, true” (SD/427).
  • “conqueror” contains “all” (SD/429).

It isn’t clear whether adjectives could generally be declined as objectives, or whether these two particular adjectives could also be used as nouns (as is the case with “all” in English).

An Adûnaic word translated “fore-cutting”, referring to the wake before a boat (PM/376). It appeared more than two decades (1968) after Tolkien’s Adûnaic Grammar in Lowdham’s Report from the 1940s (SD/413-440). It is inconsistent with the earlier grammar in two respects. First, the prepositional element ob- appears as a prefix, not as a suffix as did in the earlier grammar (SD/435). Second, it includes a short o, whereas in the earlier phonetic rules of Adûnaic, only a long is allowed (SD/423). See the entry on for further discussion.

A suffix appearing only in the name “Golden” and possibly also in . Since the element is elsewhere defined as “gold” (LotR/1114, SD/426), perhaps this suffix can be used to form from nouns in Adûnaic. Andreas Moehn suggested (/ZIM’R) it may instead be an agental suffix, a variant of .

The Adûnaic optative mood was represented by an auxiliary (SD/439). The optative mood is used to form the expression of a wish: “May you be happy in your new home”. Quenya has a similar construct: Q. “maybe, may it be that”. This Quenya element actually appears in the draft Adûnaic sentence azrē nai phurrusim akhās-ada “seas might-flow Chasm-into”, changed in the final draft to “that the seas should gush into the chasm”.

For this reason, I think both of these sentences may be examples of the optative mood, but most other authors have suggested it may be the instead. Many languages use the subjunctive for the expression of a wish as well as hypotheticals, so it is hard to say how Adûnaic may have used these verbal moods.

There is another sentence that may be an example of a “negative optative”: “Don’t [you] touch me!”, with the negative element “do not”. This sentence was translated as an English imperative command, but Tolkien did not list the imperative as one of the verbal moods of Adûnaic. Carl Hostetter and Patrick Wynne suggested (/25) that the sentence might be an optative, so that its literal meaning might be “May it be you not touch me”. This sounds plausible to me; it is possible the Adûnaic generally expresses commands with the optative mood.

Thorsten Renk suggested instead that this sentence it is a true imperative, with the imperative marker . See the entry for further discussion.

A group for continuants that do not fall into other categories. These are mostly survivals of the same sounds in Primitive Adûnaic, with the exception of breath-[h] which developed from Primitive Adûnaic <a l="ad" v="[x]"/>, which Tolkien also represented with “H” (SD/418).

As part of the phonetic development of Adûnaic, over-long vowels were sometimes produced in Primitive Adûnaic by the contact of identical vowels “where one of the merged vowels was already long” (SD/423). Such vowels also appeared as variant forms of biconsonantal roots (SD/423). In Lowdham’s Report, Tolkien used the macron (ā) for long vowels and the circumflex (â) for over-long vowels, though he was not entirely consistent in his notation.

Tolkien said these vowels were recognized “in the older language” but did not specify how they applied to speech by the time of Classical Adûnaic. It seems likely that over-long vowels would have been reduced to ordinary long vowels by the time of Classical Adûnaic. In his later writings, Tolkien used the circumflex for ordinary long vowels in Adûnaic, as he did for all of his non-Elvish languages.

The discussions uses the macron for ordinary long vowels in Primitive Adûnaic and the circumflex for ordinary long vowels in Classical Adûnaic. The primitive over-long vowels are frequently omitted, since these would eventually reduce back to ordinary long vowels.
A noun translated “hand”, given as an example of an apparent Adûnaic uniconsonantal noun, which had a but lost one of its consonants from its ancient form ✶Ad. (SD/416, 426).
A Primitive Adûnaic root glossed “hand”, the basis for the noun of the same meaning (SD/416).
The Primitive Adûnaic form of the noun “hand” (SD/426).

There are a few Adûnaic adjectives that appear to be (passive) participles, that is adjectives that are formed from verbs:

  • adj. “humbled” (SD/247) ← * “to (be) humble”
  • adj. “beloved” (SD/247) ← * “to love”

The participle suffix seems to be , as suggested by most authors (/30, , /Adûnaic, /31). There is something peculiar about these adjectives, however. First, unlike normal adjectives (SD/425), they appear after rather than before the noun they modify: Zigûrun zabathân “Sauron humbled”, Anadûnê zîrân “Númenor beloved”. Second, there is a similar suffix used to create agental nouns from verbs:

  • n. “wise man, wizard” (SD/421) ← “to understand”
  • n. * “wright, *builder” (PM/151) ← * “to build”

It is unlikely that the same suffix would be used for two very different grammatical functions, noun formation and adjective formation, both from verbs. Perhaps all of these cases are actually nouns, “*humbler”, “*lover”. The apparent use of these nouns as adjectives could be a specialized adjectival construction:

  • Zigûrun zabathân = “Sauron’s humbler” = “Sauron who is humbled”
  • Anadûnê zîrân = “Númenor’s lover” = “Númenor who is loved”

In such cases, this construct might function as a kind of subclause in the passive voice: “Sauron who is humbled”, “Númenor who is loved”. This would resolve the ambiguity between used as a participle suffix and for , but introduces a new problem however: how would Adûnaic distinguish between sentences like “Sauron who is humbled came ...” and “the humbler of Sauron came ...”?

Perhaps the location of the inflection is used to make this distinction. In the first example below, Sauron is the subject, and in the second, the humbler is the subject:

  • Zigûrun zabathân unakkha “Sauron who is humbled came ...”
  • Zigûr zabathânan unakkha “Sauron’s humbler came ...”

In the case of Anadûnê zîrân, which does not use the subjective inflection, it may be the verb’s pronominal-prefix which indicates the subject:

  • Anadûnê zîrân hikalba “Númenor who is beloved [she] fell”, agreeing with feminine Anadûnê
  • Anadûnê zîrân akalba “Númenor’s lover [it] fell”, agreeing with neuter/common zîrân

Alternately, this sentence may simply have two nouns in apposition, as indicated by the gloss of the final manuscript version:

  • Anadûnê zîrân hikalba “Anadune the beloved she fell”, agreeing with feminine Anadûnê

This is all quite speculative, but if true, the suffix -ân might always be used to form an agental noun, which can in some instances be used as if it were a participle adjective: when it follows another noun marked as the subject of the sentence.

The passive voice describes a sentence that has no explicit subject. English represents the passive voice with verbal constructs like “the pillar was broken”, leaving the person doing the breaking unspecified. Tolkien said that in Adûnaic, the passive voice was rendered by “impersonal verb forms” (SD/439). Andreas Moehn suggested () that such verbs would simply omit any subject or pronominal-prefix.

Tolkien also cryptically indicated the passive voice had “the subject in accusative” (SD/439), but Adûnaic has no accusative case. Perhaps he meant the “subject” of the English construction (really the object of the verb) was put into the object position in Adûnaic. If so, the sentence “the pillar was broken” might be rendered in Adûnaic as the subject-less sentence rahhata târik “[...] did break the pillar”.

According to Tolkien, the Adûnaic past tense was “often used as pluperfect when aorist = past, or as future perfect when aorist = future” (SD/439). This means that in a narrative like the , the aorist could be used for the ordinary past and the past tense for events even further in the past from that point in the narrative. As an example, the meaning of the Adûnaic sentence ukhaya tâidô unakkha zadnada could vary by context: “he lay down once he had come to the house” (if the narrative discusses the past) or “he lies down once he came to the house” (if the narrative discusses the present) or even “he will lay down once he comes to the house” (for narratives of the future).

Several authors identify the geminate (double consonant) verb forms as the past tense (/Adûnaic, , /26), such as: → kallaba. Based on this pattern, I would suggest the following conjugations for the past tense:

Biconsonantal VerbsDouble the last consonant, then add an -a to the verb stem “to go” → yadda “went” (SD/247)
Triconsonantal VerbsDouble the middle consonant, then add an -a to the verb stem “to fall” → kallaba “fell” (SD/247)
Derived VerbsDouble the middle consonant, inserting a stem vowel if necessary to break up clusters of more than three consonants, then change the final vowel to a short -a “to wage war” → azaggara “*waged war” (SD/247)
 “to overshadow” → *ugurruda “overshadowed”

There are attested geminate forms for all three verb classes (biconsonantal, triconsonantal and derived), but it is not clear that the attested example of a derived-verb (azaggara) is actually the past tense, so that conjugation is somewhat speculative.

Rationale: Most verb forms in the Lament can be classified as either syncopated (losing a vowel) or geminate (having a double consonant). It seems reasonable to assume that these two verb formations would be the aorist and past tenses, with the past tense functioning as a pluperfect in the text, as noted above. Choosing between the two tenses is a matter of analyzing the narrative and figuring out which instances are more likely to be a pluperfect. In the lists below, S# indicate the sentence number in the Lament.

The consistent syncopated forms are:

  • S4: Bârim an-Adûn yurahtam dâira sâibêth-mâ Êruvô “Lords of the West, they broke the Earth with assent from Eru”
  • S5: azrîya du-phursâ akhâsada “that the seas should gush into the chasm”

The consistent geminate forms are:

  • S1: kadô Zigûrun zabathân unakkha “and so Sauron he came humbled”
  • S11: adûn izindi batân tâidô ayadda “the road west once went straight”

There are several instances Tolkien vacillated between two forms:

  • S2: Êruhînim dubdam ugru-dalad “the Children of Eru fell under shadow”: dubbudam (second draft) >> dubdam (final draft)
  • S3: Ar-Pharazônun azaggara Avalôiyada “Ar-Pharazôn was warring against the Powers”: azagrāra (second draft) >> azaggara (final draft)
  • S6: Anadûnê zîrân hikalba “Númenor the beloved fell (down)”: switched back and forth between hikalba and hikallaba several times

The Lament can be divided into two stanzas, stanza one (S1-S6) describing the fall of Númenor and stanza two (S7-S13) describing the fate of the exiles after the fall. In the narrative frame of the first stanza, the geminate forms describe events that had already happened before the fall: Sauron had already come to Númenor (S1), Ar-Pharazôn had already begun his war against the Valar (S3). Similarly the syncopated forms describe events occurring at the moment of the fall: the Valar breaking the world (S4) and the seas filling the chasm left by the destruction (S5). In this context, the geminate forms make more sense as pluperfects.

In the second stanza, the geminate form describes the world’s state before the fall of Númenor: there was (once) a straight road to Valinor (S11). It is followed immediately by sentence describing the world’s state after the exile: “now all ways (are) bent” [around the now-round Earth] (S12). Again, the geminate form works better as the pluperfect.

The sentences where Tolkien vacillated between forms (S2, S6) could make sense as either a pluperfect or not. The Númenóreans’ fall under shadow (S2) could be a pluperfect with respect to fall of Númenor, or it could be within the same time frame if it is considered the proximate cause of Númenor’s destruction. The fall of Númenor itself (S6) lies between the first and second stanza: it could be a pluperfect from the perspective of the second stanza (happening before the exile) or within the same time frame if it is part of the first stanza. I treat the change of azagrāra >> azaggara (S3) as a special case, discussed separately in the entry on the .

If the roles of the aorist and past verb forms are reversed, the narrative flow breaks down. Therefore, it makes more sense that the geminate form is the past tense, used as a pluperfect throughout the Lament.

Other Theories

Carl Hostetter and Patrick Wynne suggested (/27-29) that the geminate forms are the . They base their argument on the gloss of azaggara “was warring” in the final version of the Lament. This gloss indicates this particular verb was in the continuative past, and they conclude that similar geminate forms belong to the same tense. As further evidence for their idea, they point out that Primitive Elvish sometimes used geminate forms to indicate a frequentative function (for example ᴹ✶, Ety/BAT).

While this works for azaggara, it doesn’t work well for the other geminate forms, which all glossed with the past tense. I personally believe the opposite happened: when Tolkien changed azagrāra (second draft) >> azaggara (final draft) he changed it from the continuative-past to the ordinary past tense functioning as a pluperfect, but for some reason neglected to revise its gloss. Omitting the special case of azaggara, the remaining geminate forms in the Lament work better as pluperfects, as argued above.

As a final wrinkle on this issue, Dr. Clyde Kilby suggested the geminate forms are actually intensive: Akallabeth = “The Greatly Fallen” (Tolkien & The Silmarillion, 1976); this idea is apparently based on direct communication with Tolkien. See the letter in VT25, p. 4 for further details. In this letter Eli Bar-Yahalom suggests azaggara might also be intensive, meaning “*made a great war”.

Aside from Hostetter and Wynne, there is a general consensus in the literature that the geminate forms most likely the Adûnaic past tense (/Adûnaic, , /26), although there is considerable disagreement on the exact status of azaggara.

Draft Verb Conjugations

There are several geminate (double-consonant) forms in the first draft version of the Lament of Akallabêth: unekkū “he-came”, rakkhatū “broke asunder” and phurrusim “flow” (plural). These might be early versions of the Adûnaic past tense. My theory is that the role of the aorist and past tenses in the final version of the lament were instead played by the past and tenses in the first draft of the Lament; see the entry on the draft-perfect for further discussion.

In the draft Lament, there are two singular past tense forms nekkū and rakkhatū, both ending in long ū, while the geminate form phurrusim has a different (plural?) suffix -im. It may be that in the draft past tense, the singular vowel suffix was -ū instead of the later -a. Andreas Moehn points out () that the final -ū might instead be connected to the masculine subjects, whereas Carl Hostetter and Patrick Wynne suggested (/38) that it may be connected to the fact that the subject is in the case. There isn’t really enough information available to know for sure.

There is yet another geminate form akallabi “fell in ruin”, which is the according to the theories used here; see that entry for further discussion.

In addition to for people and animals, Adûnaic sometimes uses masculine and feminine proper names for places, especially lands and cities (SD/426). Several names for Númenor and its capital city are feminine: “Westernesse, Númenor”, “The Downfallen” (Númenor after its fall) and “Armenelos”. Such formations are similar to the way a Russian might refer to Russia as female: the Motherland.

Adûnaic can also have masculine and feminine proper names for natural objects and even abstract concepts, which coexisted with the ordinary neuter words for such things: masculine “Death” beside “death”, feminine “Sun” beside "sun" and masculine “Moon” beside “moon” (SD/426). The Númenóreans regarded such personified names as actual entities. Tolkien glossed Nîlû as the “Man in the Moon” and Ûrî as the “Lady of the Sun”, so these may simply be the Adûnaic names for and (and perhaps Agân is ).

A noun meaning “gold”, the only Adûnaic word defined in The Lord of the Rings (LotR/1114).

Conceptual Development: This noun also appears in “Lowdham’s Report on the Adunaic Language” from the 1940s (SD/426).

The son of who usurped the throne to become the 25th and final ruler of Númenor, translated “Golden” (LotR/1114, S/270). His Quenya name was Tar-. Since Calion appears to mean “*Son of Light”, Ar-Pharazôn is an example of a Númenórean ruler whose Adûnaic and Quenya names had different meanings.

The first element in his name is the noun “gold”. Since Pharazôn is glossed “Golden”, the second element may be an adjectival suffix. Andreas Moehn instead suggested (/PHAR’Z) that the name means “*Golden One”, closer to its Quenya equivalent, and that the suffix -ôn is a masculine variant of the agental suffix . Either way, the name is also notable in that it does not undergo the Adûnaic when its suffix is added.

Conceptual Development: The name also appeared in “The Notion Club Papers” from the 1940s (SD/311), in some examples inflected into the case (SD/247, 428-9).

A hypothetical verbal element in the noun “conqueror” (SD/429), whose literally meaning might be “*all-ruler” (kathu-phazg-ân). Andreas Moehn suggested (/PHAZ) that it may be related to “prince” and have the meaning “to rule”, whereas Thorsten Renk suggested (/27) that it might mean “to conquer”.

A noun translated as “prince, king’s son”, given as an example of a noun with a long vowel in its final syllable that (archaically) uses the declension for a , the rare class of Strong-Ib nouns (SD/436-7). By the time of Classical Adûnaic, it could be declined as an ordinary instead.

An element appearing only in the name (UT/224). Though unglossed, her Quenya name seems to be “jewel” + “daughter”. The Adûnaic element appears elsewhere as the Adûnaic equivalent of Q. : in whose Quenya name is . These leaves the -phel to be “daughter” as suggested by several authors (/Adûnaic, /PHIL), perhaps the feminine equivalent of “son” appearing in “*Shore-son”.

Phonetically, this element does not fit the earlier Adûnaic phonetic rules of Lowdham’s Report, which state that only a long was allowed in Adûnaic (SD/423). When Tolkien wrote Lowdham’s Report, Zimraphel’s Adûnaic name was instead Zimrahil, so perhaps -hil was an earlier form of this suffix. If the suffix -phel were to be used in the phonetic context of the Adûnaic of Lowdham’s Report (Middle Adûnaic) it might have the form *-phêl. See the entry on for further discussion.

A verb translated “to-gush” or “flow” appearing in the (SD/247 SD/311), in later writings attested only in the form phursâ. This form superficially seems to be the of the triconsonantal verb phurus-. Its two draft forms phurusam > phurrusim further support the idea that the verb stem is phurus-. However, ordinarily aorist forms end in a short -a, so perhaps there is something unusual about this formation. It also lacks the usual plural verb suffix appearing in first-draft version of the Lament, which would ordinally be required to agree with the plural subject. Since phursâ appears with the or prefix du-, perhaps it is a special (infinitive?) form of the verb.

Andreas Moehn instead suggested (/PHUR) the verb stem may be phursâ- instead of phurus, so that it is a . This isn’t consistent with earlier forms, but it is possible that Tolkien changed his mind about the basic verb form.

The only actual grammatical rule we know of from Primitive Adûnaic was the formation of noun plurals. According to Tolkien, the original plural inflexion was ✶ or perhaps ✶-yi, which developed into after (SD/424).

Adûnaic plurals serve the same purpose as English plurals: to describe multiple instances of the same noun (except for natural pairs, which use the dual instead). The plural is formed with the plural inflection (SD/429). This inflection is added as a suffix to a and replaces the last vowel of a .

Plural Formation

The plural form of a noun depends largely on whether you are declining a (whose last vowel is short) or a (whose last vowel is long or a diphthong).

  • Strong Plurals: A strong noun replaces its last (short) vowel with the plural inflection î: “Elf” → Nimîr “Elves” (SD/436, WJ/386); “sea” → azrî “seas” (SD/431).
  • Weak Plurals: A weak noun adds the plural inflection î as a suffix. If the long vowel is final, the suffix either forms a diphthong or requires the use of a : “lord” → bârî “lords” (SD/251, 438); “Power, God” → Avalôi “Powers, Gods” (SD/247); “soldier” → nardûwî “soldiers” (SD/438).

These plural formations are fairly consistent. There are only a few variations.

Weak nouns ending in -ê (and -î?): In the standard Adûnaic rules for , a final long -ê absorbs the plural suffix î, making the plural form identical to the singular: “sweetheart” → izrê “sweethearts” (SD/438). To distinguish these forms, you can insert a n after the final -ê: “sweetheart” → izrênî “sweethearts” (SD/438). It is possible that the same thing can be done for weak nouns ending in -î, but Tolkien gave no such examples.

Weak nouns with archaic strong plurals: Sometimes a weak noun can use a strong plural (SD/435), especially in archaic writing. This can happen for several reasons:

  • The noun could have an archaic form that was originally strong: “man”, archaic forms †naru → (strong plural) narî “men” (SD/437). Its newer weak plural would be narû → *narûwî.
  • The noun could belong to the small class of nouns (Strong Ib, Strong IIb) that used strong declensions despite having a long vowel in its last syllable: “wife” → (strong plural) banîth “wives” (SD/437). See the section on “Archaic Strong Ib and IIb nouns” in the entry on the for further discussion. By the time of Classical Adûnaic, these nouns could be inflected with the ordinary weak plural: banâthî “wives” (SD/437).
  • Poetic writing sometimes simply uses the weak plural, perhaps to fit a meter: “road” → (strong plural) batîn “roads” (SD/247, 435). In normal speech these nouns probably use the ordinary weak plural: batânî “roads” (SD/432).

All of the above examples could also use the ordinary weak plural, so these exceptions can be safely ignored by the time of Classical Adûnaic except for their use in poetry.

Subjective Plurals

In the plural, Adûnaic distinguishes not only between the strong and weak nouns, but also between (which use the subjective declension ) and (which use the gendered plural subjective suffix ).

Neuter Subjective Plurals: Neuter plurals in the subjective simply add the subjective inflection -a as a suffix to the plural form. If the plural suffix -î appears at the end of the word, it is separated from the subjective suffix with the usual y.

  • “house” → zadîn “houses” → zadîna “houses (subjective)” (SD/430).
  • “sea” → azrî “seas” → azrîya “seas (subjective)” (SD/247, 431).

Gendered Subjective Plurals: Gendered plurals in the subjective add the gendered plural subjective suffix -im to the plural form.

  • banâth “wife” → †banîth “wives” (archaic strong plural) → †banîthim “wives (archaic subjective plural)” (SD/430).

By the time of Classical Adûnaic, most of these plurals ends in a vowel, and the suffix -im combines with the final vowel according to the Adûnaic rules for . In all such cases, the i in the suffix is absorbed by the preceding long vowel or diphthong, effectively reducing the suffix to -m:

  • “lord” → bârî “lords” → bârîm “lords (subjective)” (SD/430).
  • “soldier” → nardûwî “soldiers” → nardûwîm “soldiers (subjective)” (SD/430).
  • # “Númenórean” → Adûnâi “Númenóreans” → Adûnâim “Númenóreans (subjective)” (SD/240, PE17/18).
  • “Power, God” → Avalôi “Powers, Gods” → Avalôim “Powers, Gods (subjective)” (SD/241).
  • “sweetheart” → izrê “sweethearts” → izrêm “sweethearts (subjective)” (SD/438).

The last example (izrê) has another plural form. As noted above, plurals of nouns ending in -ê (and perhaps also those ending in -î) can use a n to help distinguish the singular and plural forms. In such cases, the gendered plural subjective suffix -im is added to this variant plural form with the linking n:

  • “sweetheart” → izrênî “sweethearts” → izrênîm “sweethearts (subjective)” (SD/438).

Gendered Subjective Plurals with Syncope: The gendered strong-I nouns (those ending in a consonant preceded by a short vowel) are an exception to the above rules. Such nouns first undergo the Adûnaic before the subjective suffix -im is added, so that the last short vowel of the noun is lost instead of being replaced by the plural inflection î:

  • “Elf” → Nimrim “Elves (subjective)” instead of **Nimîrim (SD/436).
  • “smith” → tamrim “smiths (subjective)” instead of **tamîrim (SD/436).

Where the syncope cannot occur, the subjective suffix -im is added to the normal plural form, as above:

  • # “Child of God” → Êruhîn “Children of God” (SD/311) → Êruhînim “Children of God (subjective)” (SD/247).

Irregular Plurals

There are several attested Adûnaic plurals that do not fit the plural formation rules described above.

Strong plurals with medial y: For strong nouns that have an isolated medial y, this y disappears when the last vowel is replaced by the plural inflection -î-, so that the plural inflection forms a diphthong with the second-to-last vowel:

  • “land” → zâin “lands” (SD/423, 435).

This irregularity can be explained by the ancient phonetic development of Adûnaic, in which .

  • ✶zāyan → (plural) ✶zāyīn > zā-īn > zâin (SD/423).

Variant plurals with short i: In a few places, Tolkien has plurals with a short i where a long î would be expected from the rules above:

  • bâr “lord” → bâri “lords” (SD/251).
  • bâr “lord” → bârim “lords (subjective)” (SD/247).

In Lowdham’s Report, these examples appear as regular plurals with a long î:

  • bâr “lord” → bârî “lords” (SD/438).
  • bâr “lord” → bârîm “lords (subjective)” (SD/438).

These variations may be remnants of Tolkien’s older conception of the Adûnaic plural, which frequently used a short i instead of a long one (see the entry on the ).

The suffix appears consistently at the end of verbs that have a plural subject, marking the plurality of the verb to agree with that subject. The suffix appears whether or not the verb has a pronominal-prefix, and appears in both the draft and later stages of Adûnaic.

There is only one example where the plural-verb suffix does not appear: the pseudo- verb form phursâ of “to gush, flow”. This (along with its gloss “to-gush”) lends weight to the idea that it may be a special form, perhaps an infinitive.

According to Tolkien, Adûnaic “employs prefixions more frequently than suffixion” in word-formation (SD/417). This statement is at odds with the available evidence, however. The endings for are all suffixes, Adûnaic makes use of prepositional suffixes, and most inflections for occur at the end of the word. The only clear prefixal formations are and the genitive prefix .

It is possible that Tolkien was referring to the process of extending primitive . Primitive Eldarin extended roots by adding suffixal elements, such as the Elvish root √ “light; shine” which was extended to √ “glory, radiance” (PE18/87). Perhaps Primitive Adûnaic extended roots by adding prefixes. If so, this word formation rule may refer instead to Primitive Adûnaic word formation, but we have no example of such extensions, either prefixal or suffixal.

In English, prepositions are short words like “from” or “to” used to construct small phrases expressing some relationship to other elements in the sentence. The name of this grammatical function is biased towards its use in European languages, where such elements usually appear at the beginning of the phrase. In Adûnaic, the “prepositions” are instead expressed as suffixes added to the end of the word (SD/435):

  • nardûn nakkha kadarô “the soldier came from the city”
  • Ar-Pharazônun yadda Arminalêthada “Ar-Pharazon went to Armenelos”.

The noun modified by the prepositional suffix is always in the normal case (SD/429). Furthermore, if the noun ends in -u or -i and the prepositional suffix begins in a vowel, the usual w or y is inserted between the two vowels:

  • Ar-Pharazônun azaggara Avalôiyada (Avalôi-y-ada) “Ar-Pharazôn was warring against the Powers” (SD/247)
  • Bârim an-Adûn yurahtam dâira sâibêth-mâ Êruvô (Êru-w-ô) “Lords of the West, they broke the Earth with assent from Eru” (SD/247)

In the second example, the letter “v” is properly pronounced when Adûnaic is represented with English letters (SD/434). Although not discussed by Tolkien, other vowel combinations in prepositions probably follow the usual rules for Adûnaic .

The known prepositional suffixes appearing in the (SD/247) and “Lowdham’s Report on the Adunaic Language” (SD/429) from the 1940s are:

  • “to, towards”
  • -dalad “under, beneath”
  • “with”
  • “on”
  • “from”
  • “at”
  • “away” [speculative]

A few more prepositional elements appear in Tolkien’s later writings (PM/376), but these were used as prefixes:

  • “behind”
  • “before”

Draft Adûnaic: In Tolkien’s early Adûnaic drafts, most these prepositional suffixes were instead examples of the , with further modifications for the number and gender of the noun. In later Adûnaic grammar, Tolkien abandoned this case syntax and switched to simple, immutable prepositional suffixes, as discussed above.

word.v: primitive Elvish short [e] and [o] became [i] and [u]
word.notes: Loan words from Elvish with short vowels ĕ and ŏ generally replace them in Adûnaic with i and u respectively, though in some case either could become a instead (SD/414). It seems this rule applies both to early and ancient borrowings.

ref.v: primitive Elvish short [e] and [o] became [i] and [u]

word.notes:
Most attested Adûnaic pronouns appear as prefixes to verbs. When a pronoun is the subject of a verb, it is prefixed directly to the verb form. For example, the Adûnaic feminine singular pronoun is “she” and the form of the verb “to fall” is kalba “falls”, so “she falls” in Adûnaic would be hikalba (SD/247).

There appear to be several circumstances in which a pronominal-prefix can be used with verbs.

1) The pronominal-prefix could be the only subject:

  • usaphda “he understood” (SD/421)
  • bâ kitabdahê “Don’t [you] touch me!” (SD/250)

2) There can be a separate subject noun in the . When the subject is in the normal case, the pronominal-prefix is always required (SD/429):

  • adûn izindi batân tâidô ayadda “the road west [it] once went straight” (SD/247)
  • Anadûnê zîrân hikalba “Númenor the beloved she fell (down)” (SD/247)

3) There can be a separate subject noun in the case. When the subjective case is used in combination with a pronominal-prefix, the subject is emphatic (SD/429):

  • kadô Zigûrun zabathân unakkha “and so Sauron he came humbled” (SD/247)
  • bârun ukallaba “it was the lord who fell” (SD/429)

The pronominal-prefix is optional if the subject noun is declined into the case. Where omitted, the subject is not emphatic:

  • bârun kallaba “the lord fell” (SD/429)
  • “the Children of Eru fell under shadow” (SD/247)

Apart from the subjective case, the only other known situation where the pronominal prefix can be omitted is with , which have no subject.

There are no attested independent pronouns in Adûnaic. Where pronominal elements appear, they are attached to verbs or prepositional suffixes. These elements form an almost complete pronoun paradigm:

PersonSingularPlural
1st person “me” “us”
2nd person “you”?
3rd person neuter “it” “they”
3rd person masculine “he” “they”
3rd person feminine “she”* “they”

The first person pronouns are only attested as objects: kitabdahê “[you] touch me” (SD/250), nênud “on us” (SD/247); it isn’t clear whether they can be used as subjects. The other pronouns are only attested as subjects and it is not clear whether they can be used as objects. The 3rd person feminine plural pronoun is not attested, but generalizing from the neuter and masculine plural pronouns, the form *yi seems likely.

The second person pronoun is attested only in the phrase bâ kitabdahê “Don’t [you] touch me”. It is not glossed, but many authors have suggested it is probably the second person pronoun (/Adûnaic, , /18). It resembles the Primitive Elvish 2nd person familiar pronoun ✶, to which it might be related. If so, it is probably a singular pronoun; whether it can also be used for the plural is unclear. None of the other Adûnaic pronouns have clear Elvish cognates, so the resemblance could just be a coincidence.

Finally, Thorsten Renk suggested (/18) that may instead be a marker for the imperative. He suggested an invented word !ni for “I, me” to use for the 1st persons singular pronoun instead (/18), as a cognate of Q. .

The Adûnaic p-series of homorganic consonants included the labial consonants and the semi-vowel [w], which Tolkien often classified with labials. They were mostly survivals of the Primitive Adûnaic (SD/418).

A series of labial consonants in Primitive Adûnaic. Unlike the other series, it had no <a l="pad" v="voiceless-continuants"/>, though Tolkien indicated it may once have had one, a voiceless w, which prehistorically became the voiceless velar continuant <a l="pad" v="[x]"/> (SD/417).
A noun translated “breath” and fully declined as an example of a Weak I noun (SD/431).
A possible element in the verb “to wage war”, perhaps a causative suffix, as suggested by Carl Hostetter and Patrick Wynne (/24).

A noun translated “dog” and fully declined as an example of a Strong II noun (SD/437). It is also used as an example of a common-noun that can be altered to masculine and feminine forms rabô “male dog” and rabê “bitch” (SD/434).

A verb appearing in the with the past-tense translations “broke” and “rent” (SD/247, VT24/12), so meaning “to break, rend”. In the final version of the Lament it appeared as yurahtam “they rent”. The initial element of this form is the 3rd persons masculine plural suffix yu- “they”, while its final element is the plural verbal suffix , both in agreement with the plural subject Bârîm “Lords”. This leaves the basic verb form rahta, which is the tense according to the theories used here.

In the previous (second draft) version of the Lament, the verb form was urahta with the 3rd persons masculine singular suffix u- “he”, and no plural suffix -m. This is consistent with the subject in this version, which was the singular Bârun “Lord”.

Carl Hostetter and Patrick Wynne suggested (/22) that this verb may be related to Q. “to break” (MC/223). It could also be related to the contemporaneous ᴹQ. “to break asunder” (Ety/SKAT).

Conceptual Development: In the first draft of the Lament, the form was rakkhatū, indicating the earliest form of the verb may have had the verb stem rakhat- instead of later rahat-.

Once the basic pattern of a primitive word was established by , it could undergo further modifications to produce the final form of the word. There were two kinds of further modifications: ( and ) and ( and ) (SD/424).

Tolkien states that “any given derivative never shows two of the one [i.e. same] kind of variation at the same time” (SD/424), where the vowel modifications were one kind of process and the consonant modifications another. Thus, any given word would have at most two modifications: one vowel modification and one consonant modification. Tolkien does list a few examples where both kinds of modifications occur, such as ✶kullūb < √KULUB (SD/425) with both consonant doubling and vowel lengthening.

Starting from the basic biconsonantal patterns (✶zir(i), ✶izri, ✶izir) and triconsonantal patterns (✶kal(a)b, ✶kalb(a), ✶aklab, ✶akalb(u) and ✶daw’r), there were a large number of possible words could be produced through these further modifications, especially when was included. For any given root, only a few of the possible variations were realized as actual words, however (SD/425).

Primitive roots were the basic building blocks of Primitive Adûnaic words. In Lowdham’s Report, Tolkien used the term “bases” instead of roots. Words that are etymologically related can be attributed to a common root, but it is unlikely such a root served a genuine grammatical function in Primitive Adûnaic. True Primitive Adûnaic roots had either two consonants () or three consonants () combined with a (a, i or u), for example: ✶Ad. √ “love, desire” or ✶Ad. √ “fall”. There were also s used for affixes, inflections and pronominal stems, but these were not considered true roots (SD/415-6).

Words could be formed from roots using various rules describing the possible word patterns. There were probably grammatical rules underlying these patterns, but they can no longer be discerned. A common pattern was to have the characteristic vowel after the first and second consonants; such words were called the of the root (SD/422), for example ✶ziri or ✶kalab. Other patterns were variations on the full form.

An element appearing in the name “Foam-flower”, attested in later writings (1968) as roth (PM/369, 376). This later form is incompatible with the earlier phonetic rules of Lowdham’s Report from the 1940s, which allowed only long in Adûnaic words. If this word were used in the phonetic context of Lowdham’s Report (Middle Adûnaic), it should be rôth, and in these earlier texts, the Adûnaic name of Eärendi’s ship was Rôthinzil with a long ô (SD/360). Even in later writings, Tolkien lists róþ ([rōθ] = rôth) as one of its possible forms (PM/369). See the entry on for further discussion.

The Adûnaic name of Eärendil’s ship “Foam-flower”, of the same meaning (S/249). This name appears in earlier writings as Rôthinzil with a long ô (SD/360). Its later form is a violation of the phonetic rules laid out by Tolkien in Lowdham’s Report, which said that the vowels and could only be long in Adûnaic (SD/423). The later form could be an Anglicanized or a Westronized form (where a short could appear), or it could indicate that Tolkien changed his mind about Adûnaic phonetic rules. Some linguistic notes from the 1930s suggest Tolkien at one point considered making the name Quenya (P19/49).
A word glossed “shout” (SD/426). Andreas Moehn suggested (/RUKH) that it may be a verb rûkh- “to shout”, but it appears in a list of nouns, so I think it likelier that it is noun form.

This root, glossed “scar, score, furrow”, appeared as part of a discussion of the origin of the Sindarin word S. “foam” appearing in the name “Star-foam” (PM/368-371). Tolkien was uncertain whether this Sindarin word could coexist with its homophone S. “copper-coloured”, and investigated the possibility that Elros was instead derived from a Beorian word “foam”. According to Christopher Tolkien, his father was forced to abandon this line of reasoning when he remembered that the unrelated name S. also contained this element, forcing it to be of Sindarin rather than Beorian origin (SD/371).

Despite all this, the related Adûnaic word Ad. roth “foam” survived in The Silmarillion in the Adûnaic name “Foam-flower” of Earendil’s ship. Therefore, perhaps this root remains valid. According to Tolkien, this root originally had to do with ploughs and ploughing, and was later used for the white crest of waves by analogy with the churning dirt of a furrow (PM/376).

A noun translated “assent” (SD/247). The second element of this word is probably “word” as suggested by several authors (/22, /BITH). It isn’t clear what the first element means.

Conceptual Development: In the draft versions of the Lament of Akallabêth, the form of this word was sōbēth (SD/311).

This word is attested only in , whose Quenya name is (UT/223). The first element of the Quenya name seems to be “shore”, so the first element of his Adûnaic name probably has the same meaning, as suggested by several authors (/22, /Adûnaic, /SAK’L).

The son of Ar- and the 22nd ruler of Númenor, whose Quenya name was Tar- (UT/223). Tolkien didn’t translate either name, but his Quenya name seems to mean something like “*Shore-son” ( “shore” + “-son”) and his Adûnaic name may have a similar meaning, as suggested by several authors (/22, /Adûnaic, /SAK’L). If so, the initial element * would mean “shore” and the suffix would mean “-son”.

The interpretation of the second element is less certain than the first. For example, Carl Hostetter and Patrick Wynne suggested (/11) that is Quenya name Falassion is actually a genitive plural meaning “of the Coasts” and does not involve “-son” at all. They suggested the final -thôr may instead mean “one” or “lord” (/23).
An otherwise unexplained root Tolkien gave to illustrate a pronunciation example. It may not be a real root.
A word Tolkien used to illustrate Adûnaic pronunciation without giving its meaning (SD/421).
A Primitive Adûnaic root glossed “understand” (SD/416), the basis for the verb “to understand” and the noun “wise man” (SD/421).

A verb attested only in the form usaphda “he understood”, an inflection with the 3rd person masculine pronominal prefix u- (SD/421). Archaically its aorist form underwent phonetic changes to become †saptha, but it was later reformed to be consistent with other inflections of the verb (such as the tense *sapphada).
The primitive form of “wise man, wizard”, derived from the root ✶Ad. √ (SD/421). Its final element may be a primitive form of the agental suffix .

A noun translated “wise man, wizard” given as an example of the phonetic development of primitive aspirates in contact with stops (SD/421). According to Tolkien, it was pronounced [safθān], indicating that the combination pth would be pronounced as a voiceless labial fricative [f] followed by a voiceless dental fricative [θ]. Given the phonetic rules of Adûnaic, most voiceless stops would be pronounced as fricatives before another fricative in Classical Adûnaic.

The Adûnaic number “two” (SD/428). It seems likely that it is related to Q. “two”, as suggested by Carl Hostetter and Patrick Wynne (/22), though it is unclear how the initial s- might have developed in the Adûnaic. It may also be related to the Adûnaic dual suffix , as suggested by Andreas Moehn (/SAT).

word.v: short diphthongs [ai] and [au] monophthongized to [ē] and [ō]
word.notes: Where <a l="pad" v="a-fortification"/> and vowel contacts produced the primitive <a l="pad" v="diphthongs"/> ✶[au], ✶[ai], these monophthongized into the simple long vowels [ē] and [ō] (SD/423). This was the means whereby these vowels were introduced into Adûnaic. This rule only applied to short diphthongs, since later long <a l="ad" v="diphthongs"/> survived unchanged (SD/423). According to Tolkien, the primitive diphthong were only found “in the oldest texts”, so this must have been an early change, though the rule seems to have remained functional throughout the development of Adûnaic.

ref.v: short diphthongs [ai] and [au] monophthongized to [ē] and [ō]

word.notes: Sibilants are consonants made with a hissing sound, in Classisal Adûnaic <a l="ad" v="[s]"/> and <a l="ad" v="[z]"/>. These were either survivals of the same Primitive Adûnaic sounds, or developed from voiceless and voiced Primitive Adûnaic palatals, which Tolkien labeled the <a l="pad" v="c-series"/> (SD/418). Tolkien did not define Adûnaic sibilants as its own group, but the discussion here does so to simplify discussion of the Primitive Adûnaic <a l="pad" v="c-series"/>.

Tolkien never specifically discussed single-vowel Primitive Adûnaic words, but there are numerous examples of words from s that have only a single characteristic vowel. This vowel is always in the normal position between the first and second consonant. For example, the primitive word ✶ “crow” fits this pattern, and classical Adûnaic words like “word”, “lord”, “fool” and “breath” were most likely derived from single vowel biconsonantal primitive forms, from the roots ✶Ad. √BITH, *√BAR, *√NUPH and *√PUH.

The case for single-vowel words derived from s is more complex. A word like **kal’b from the root ✶Ad. √KALAB is not possible, since clusters are not allowed as the of Primitive Adûnaic words. There is, however, one example of a primitive triconsontal word with a single vowel: ✶Ad. √ > ✶ > Ad. “gloom”. It seems likely that such primitive single-vowel triconsonantal words were only possible when the semi-vowels [w] or [j] were the middle consonant, since these would develop into vowels when .
As with English, the Adûnaic singular form is the unmodified form of the noun, and refers to a single item. It is the form from which other forms are derived (SD/427).

word.v: spirant [x] became breath [h] except before [s] and for double [xx]
word.notes:
The Primitive Adûnaic spirant ✶[x] (which Tolkien spelled “H”) in most cases developed into a “breath-H” [h] (SD/419). It was retained before [s] and as a double-consonant [xx]. Given that the aspirate [kʰ] did not also develop into [h], this change must have happened before ([kʰ] > [x]).

Elsewhere Tolkien indicated that the changes in [ɣ] happened in “parallel with the softening of the voiceless equivalent H [x] to the breath-H” (SD/420), putting all of these change roughly at the same stage of development.

ref.v: spirant [x] became breath [h] except before [s] and for double [xx]
spirant [x] became breath [h] except before [s] and for double [xx]

word.notes: A classification of Primitive Adûnaic consonants for which the flow of air is obstructed. This group is further divided into voiceless, voiced and aspirated stops.

Classical Adûnaic consonants can be classified into groups by their method of pronunciation. The discussion here uses the category of “stops and spirants” to describe the consonants descended from Primitive Adûnaic <a l="pad" v="stops"/>.

When a stop (voiced, voiceless or aspirate) appeared after an aspirate [pʰ], [tʰ], [kʰ], the aspiration was transferred to the end, devoicing the following stop in the process. The examples given by Tolkien were the combinations [pʰt], [pʰd], [pʰtʰ] which all became [pʰtʰ] (SD/421).

Tolkien noted that combinations of stops were rare (SD/421), most likely because consonants pairs usually included at least one continuant, as discussed under . The only example he gave of this development was the word , phonetically [safθān].

Furthermore, he stated that where this development was the result of verbal or noun inflection, the change was often reverted for consistency with other noun or verb forms. The example he gave was the verb * whose aorist tense would have become saphda > saptha under normal phonetic development, but was reformed back to saphda (SD/421), presumably by comparison to other forms such as the past tense *sapphada.

This change preceded other changes (aspirates to spirants) and was therefore probably early. Note that aspirates in ancient Quenya caused a similar change, except that the preceding aspirate lost its aspiration and became a voiceless stop (PE19/87).
word.related: probably (since Tolkien did not mention palatals in this rule) happened after

word.notes:
Polysyllabic nouns whose last syllable contains a short vowel are considered strong nouns. Strong nouns generally alter this final vowel, the so-called “variable vowel”, when declined into various (SD/430). Primitively, strong nouns were derived from the of a or one of its simple variants, but by the time of Classical Adûnaic, the strong declensions applied to most nouns with a short final vowel (SD/425).

The strong nouns could be further subdivided into two groups (SD/430), those ending in a single consonant preceded by a short vowel (Strong I) and those ending in a short vowel preceded by one or more consonants (Strong II), for example: “mast” (Strong I), “night” (Strong II), “jewel” (Strong II). Often the second-to-last syllable of a Strong I noun has the same short vowel as the last syllable, so that it undergoes the Adûnaic when a suffix is added, losing its final vowel.

Neuter Nouns

With neuter strong nouns, the variable vowel changes when declined in the and cases, as well as for (SD/430-1). Since the vowels and are always long in Adûnaic, the only possible variable vowels are a, i and u.

  • Subjective: The variable vowel is a-fortified, changing as follows: a ⇒ â, i ⇒ ê and u ⇒ ô. See the discussions under and for the phonetic developments leading to these changes.
  • Objective: The variable vowel is changed to u. If the variable vowel is already u, there is usually no change (but see below).
  • Plural: The variable vowel is changed to î. For the subjective plural, the subjective inflection is added as a suffix to the plural form in the same way as it does for weak nouns. For Strong II nouns ending in a vowel, the usual y is used to separate the final plural î from the suffixal -a, and the result is -îya.

For the dual form of strong nouns, the usual dual suffix is added. For most Strong I nouns, the Adûnaic also applies so that the variable vowel is lost. For Strong II nouns ending in -i or -u, the appropriate is inserted between the variable vowel and the suffix, y or w respectively. If the dual noun is used in the subjective case, the a in the dual suffixed is lengthened to -ât, as if it were a singular strong noun being declined into the subjective.

The full set of declensions is:

Some notes:

[1] For Strong I nouns where the variable vowel is a u, there is no change in the objective case. Alternately, Strong I nouns with a final vowel u sometimes form the objective with a syncope (if they allow it) and a suffixal -u: sulum → sulmu (SD/435). This formation can also occur with Strong I nouns that have the vowels a or i, but less commonly.

[2] For Strong I nouns where the second-to-last vowel is either long () or followed by a consonant cluster (), the Adûnaic syncope is not allowed and the variable vowel is retained in the dual (SD/430). This is probably also true when the second-to-last and last vowels are different (e.g. ), but there are no clear examples.

[3] For Strong II nouns ending in -u instead of -i, the is w instead of y, as usual: ugru → ugruwat. In archaic writing, the dual suffix would replace the final -i/-u instead of using a glide consonant. At a later (Exilic?) stage, the dual suffix came to be regarded as -ât, so that the a was long in both the normal and subjective duals (SD/431).

[4] Strong II nouns whose final vowel is -a do not use a glide consonant. The dual suffix merges with the final -a to produce -ât, so that the normal and subjective duals are identical (though they were distinct in archaic writings, at the time when the dual suffix replaced the final vowel). Such nouns were so common that at later (Exilic?) stage, the dual suffix came to be regarded as -ât for all nouns (SD/431), as previously mentioned in note [3].

[5] For Strong II nouns, the final vowel in plurals became the plural affix -î. In the subjective case, the subjective inflection was suffixed to this -î, with the usual glide consonant y after the î.

Gendered Nouns

Gendered nouns were usually weak, because most gendered nouns had a long vowel in their final syllable (SD/436). This less true of common nouns, more true of masculine nouns and almost always true of feminine nouns. However, there are a few gendered nouns with short final vowels that are declined as strong nouns, for example: “girl” (Strong I), †naru “male” (Strong II, an archaic form of ), “dog” (Strong II).

The strong gendered nouns are declined in the same way as the strong neuter nouns except for in the subjective case:

  • Subjective Singular: The gendered Strong I nouns use the gendered subjective suffixes (common), (feminine) and (masculine), together with the usual Adûnaic (SD/436). For gendered Strong II nouns, the subjective suffix is reduced to -n for all genders. This is because masculine Strong II nouns end in -u, feminine in -i and neuter in -a, so that “replacing” the final vowel with the appropriate suffix is the same as adding -n (SD/437).
  • Subjective Plural: The subjective plural uses the gendered plural subjective suffix with the usual Adûnaic for Strong I nouns. In the case of Strong II nouns, the final vowel is replaced by -îm (SD/436), or more accurately the suffix -im is added to the normal plural form ending -î.

The full set of declensions for gendered strong nouns is:
