word.notes:
A Doriathrin adjective for “grey” written heðu in The Etymologies, and derived from the primitive form ᴹ✶ [kʰitʰwa] (Ety/KHIS). This word illustrates several interesting phonetic changes in Ilkorin.

  1. The [i] became [e] before the final [a].
  2. Both the : [kʰ-] > [x-] and [-tʰ-] > [-θ-].
    1. Later the .
    2. Meanwhile the medial [-θ-] voiced to [-ð-] (“dh”).
  3. The primitive final [a] was lost.
  4. Afterwards, the resulting final [w] became [u].

In most other Doriathrin words, a final [u] from [w] further developed into [o]; it is unclear why this change did not occur here.
A noun glossed “captain” derived from the root ᴹ√ “command” (EtyAC/KHES). The language of this word is unclear; Carl Hostetter and Patrick Wynne indicated it might be ?Bel. for Beleriandic = Ilkorin.

A Doriathrin noun for “fog” written hiðum in The Etymologies, and derived from the primitive form ᴹ✶ [kʰitʰme] (Ety/KHIS, EtyAC/KHIS). This word illustrates several interesting phonetic changes in Ilkorin.

  1. Both the : [kʰ-] > [x-] and [-tʰ-] > [-θ-].
    1. Later the .
    2. Meanwhile the medial [-θ-] voiced to [-ð-] (“dh”).
  2. The primitive final [e] was lost.
  3. Afterwards, the resulting final [m] became syllabic and developed into [-um].
A Doriathrin noun for “lady” attested only as an element in the name (Ety/NEL). It probably had essentially the same derivation as its Noldorin cognate N. (Ety/KHER).

The Ilkorindi were among the Elves who went on the great journey but chose to remain behind in Beleriand when the rest of their kin left for Valinor (LR/112). After this, the Ilkorin languages diverged from those of the other Eldar. As most of the Ilkorins were members of the third tribe, their languages were originally related to the (Middle) Telerin language spoken by the Sea Elves (LR/175). After the Noldorin exile to Beleriand, the Noldorin and Ilkorin languages strongly influenced one another (LR/177), but judging from the Tree of Tongues (LR/170), Ilkorin had more influence on Noldorin than the other way around. Regardless, many of the later phonetic changes of Noldorin resemble those of Ilkorin. After the fall of Beleriand, it seems that most of the Ilkorindi joined with the Noldor returning to the West, but a few remained behind, slowly fading away under the doom of Mandos (LR/178).

A preposition “from, away” marked as both Ilkorin (Ety/ƷŌ̆; PE21/60) and Doriathrin (EtyAC/ƷŌ̆). It developed from primitive ᴹ✶ʒō̆ (Ety/WŌ), with the initial [ɣ] becoming [g]. It was also used as patronymic, as in go-Thingol “*child of Thingol” (Ety/ƷŌ̆).

Conceptual Development: This preposition may be a restoration of the Gnomish patronymic G. . In Tolkien’s later writings, Common Eldarin: Noun Structure (EVS2) from around 1950 mentioned a similar Beleriandic preposition ho “from” derived from ✶ʒō̆ which influenced a patronymic hon based on {✶jond- >>} ✶ʒond- “son”. This late appearance was shortly before he abandoned Ilkorin/Beleriandic entirely.
A word for “a blow with an axe” in Early Noldorin Word-lists of the 1920s derived from primitive ᴱ✶skantá (PE13/147).
Apparently a feminine suffix attested only in the name (Ety/LUK).
Apparently a feminine suffix attested in the name “(Woman of) Secret Shadow” (Ety/THUR) and the noun “queen” (Ety/TĀ).

A suffix appearing in almost all attested Ilkorin plurals.

Conceptual Development: This suffix is the same as the most common Gnomish plural suffix (GG/10).
In Ilkorin an initial [j] (= “y”) vanished. This change is described in the Comparative Tables (PE19/19) and there are several examples in The Etymologies (see below).

It seems that [w] was lost between an initial [k] or [g] and a following [o]. There is one example of this change for [kwo-]: ᴹ√ > [kwāme > kwōm(e) >] (Ety/KWAM). For the case of [gwo-], the clearest example is archaic † “together”, for which Tolkien said: “in Ilk. owing to coalescence of gwo, ʒo (in go) this prefix was lost” (Ety/WŌ). The other examples of this rule involve an initial [w] becoming [gw], and then a resulting [gwo-] becoming [go-] (see below). This change was suggested by Helge Fauskanger (AL-Ilkorin/gôd, gôr, gwo-).
Based on the example ᴹ✶ > Ilk. (Ety/MORÓK), it seems that the initial combination [mr-] became [br-] in Ilkorin after the unstressed vowel vanished.

These developments are clearly described on the Comparative Tables (PE19/19). In The Etymologies, there are no examples [ŋ-], but the examples for [ɣ-] are numerous (see below).

Conceptual Development: In later notes on the development of Beleriandic [Ilkorin] ʒ and ñ written around 1950, Tolkien first described the same changes as above, but then revised the development of initial [ɣ-] to become [h-] (PE18/103-4, note #148). There are no attested examples of this revised development, however, and Tolkien abandoned the Ilkorin/Beleriandic language soon after these notes were written.

This Ilkorin phonetic rule is similar to sound changes that occurred in Old Noldorin. The likely development was that the stops first became aspirates [pʰ], [tʰ] and [kʰ], after which the initial [s] was lost and then the [f-], [θ-] and [x-] (> [h-]), as indicated on the Comparative Tables (PE19/20). In The Etymologies, the only attested examples of this rule involve [st-] > [θ-] (see below).

This change did not occur where the initial [s] became syllabic: compare ᴹ√SPÁLAS > Ilk. (Ety/PHAL).

This Ilkorin phonetic rule is similar to sound changes that occurred in later Old Sindarin but not in contemporaneous Old Noldorin. Afterwards, the initial [s] was lost to leave only the voiceless initial consonants, as indicated on the Comparative Tables (PE19/20). There are no attested examples of this development in The Etymologies.

Conceptual Development: In later linguistic notes from around 1950, the “Beleriandic” development seems to have been initial [s-] to [θ-] instead: “sr > thr (þr)” (PE18/94), whereas simple initial y, w, l, r always became unvoiced (PE18/105). Both these developments were similar to the rules of Old Noldorin and Noldorin, so perhaps Tolkien switched the phonetic rules between the two languages; the later Sindarin language had the same development as the Ilkorin of the 1930s. This revision occurred shortly before Tolkien abandoned the Ilkorin language entirely.
This rule is described on the Comparative Tables along with the unvoicing effects of the initial [s] (PE19/20-21), but in The Etymologies the only examples are [st-] > [θ-] (see below).
In Ilkorin an initial [w] became [gw], as was also the case in Noldorin. This change is described in the Comparative Tables (PE19/19) and there are numerous examples in The Etymologies (see below).

In the Comparative Tables, an initial aspirate [kʰ] developed into [h] (PE19/18). This was also true when the aspirate developed from an initial [s]: ᴹ✶sk > [kʰ >] Ilk. h (PE19/20). There are several examples of this development in The Etymologies (see below).

In the Comparative Tables, where the initial aspirate [kʰ] appeared before an [l], [r], [w], the result was a voiceless [l̥], [r̥], [w̥] (PE19/18, 21). This was also true when the aspirate developed from an initial [s]: ᴹ✶skw > [kʰw >] Ilk. hw (PE19/20). There is only one example of this rule in The Etymologies: ᴹ✶ > Dor. (EtyAC/KHARÁS).

Most likely this development occurred after , ([kʰ-] > [x-]), and was part of the general trend whereby . This development did not occur for [j] (“y”), since either [j] was lost after initial velars or ; Tolkien vacillated on the exact development of [j] after initial velars.

word.v: initial nasals usually vanished before stops
word.notes:
The Comparative Tables indicate that primitive initial combinations of nasals and voiced stops generally lost their nasal sound (PE19/20). The same rule applied to “Beleriandic” development in Tolkien’s linguistic notes from around 1950 (PE18/103-4). There are a number of examples of this development in The Etymologies (see below).

However, the actual development in the Comparative Tables shows ✶mb > Ilk. b, mb; ✶nd > Ilk. d, nd; ✶ng > Ilk. g, ng. This indicates that while the normal development was to simple stops, in some case the development could be different. There are a number of examples of such alternate development in The Etymologies. The Doriathrin derivatives of the root ᴹ√ all show variations beginning with both g- and ng-, while the Doriathrin derivatives ᴹ√ all begin with ng-. Similarly, ᴹ√ > Dor. , with a simple nasal instead of a simple stop.

All the examples of this variation are Doriathrin and occur before the vowel [o]. There is an example of a Doriathrin noun with ✶[ŋg-] > [g-] before [a], however: ᴹ√ > Dor. . Furthermore, there are no examples of this variation for [nd-], whereas ᴹ✶ > Dor. . Therefore the conditions of this variant development may be where [mb-] and [ŋg-] precede the vowel be [o] (and perhaps [u]) and the variation may be limited to the Doriathrin dialect.

In the case of [mb-], it seems the variation leads to the simple nasal [m-]. It may be that ng- is an orthographic representation of the simple velar nasal [ŋ-], so that in both cases the nasal-stop cluster reduced to a simple nasal for the variation.

ref.v: initial nasals usually vanished before stops

word.notes:
In the Ilkorin phonetic developments described in The Etymologies, it appears that an initial palatalized velar became a non-palatalized dental, as noted by Helge Fauskanger (AL-Ilkorin/telf), similar to the medial development of labialized velars described in the Comparative Tables (PE19/23). There are two examples: Ilk. derived from the root ᴹ√ (Ety/GYEL) and Ilk. derived from the root ᴹ√ (Ety/KYELEP). It seems likely the rule applied to other initial labialized velars as well.

Conceptual Development: This rule contradicts the initial developments described in the Comparative Tables, where [j] was lost after initial velars (PE19/18-20). It seems that Tolkien changed his mind between writing the tables and beginning work on The Etymologies. In some later tables on “Belariandric”, it seems Tolkien toyed with restoring this development (PE18/105): gy > g (not d), but he soon after abandoned the Ilkorin language completely.

word.v: [j] was lost after initial velars and dentals
word.notes: In the Ilkorin phonetic developments described in the Comparative Tables, initial labialized velar lost their labialization but remained velars (PE19/18-20), and similarly for dentals (PE19/22). This change is not attested in The Etymologies, where it seems that .

ref.v: [j] was lost after initial velars and dentals

word.notes: The Doriathrin word for the “Moon” developed from the primitive name ᴹ✶ (Ety/I²), though it is unclear how the [st] developed. Perhap it was of the same origin as “silver light, starlight” (Ety/SIL).

A Doriathrin noun for “silver light, starlight”, also given as istel, which developed from the root ᴹ√ (Ety/SIL). Tolkien said that it was probably originally a (ancient?) Quenya word learned from Melian. This apparently this means its development was unusual. Along with the identical “Moon”, it is the only Ilkorin noun with a medial [st]. Helge Fauskanger suggested it must have developed by a strengthening of [s] to [st]. It may also be another example of a development from syllabic [ṣ], though elsewhere .

A rejected Doriathrin noun for “babe” developed from the root ᴹ√ (EtyAC/LAP). Its Quenya cognate ᴹQ. suggests a primitive form of *✶lapsē, but elsewhere a medial [ps] became [ss] in Ilkorin, as with < ᴹ✶.

An adjective meaning “fresh, lively” developed from the primitive form ᴹ✶ (Ety/LÁYAK). It is a good example of how in Ilkorin, as suggested by Helge Fauskanger (AL-Ilkorin/laig). This allowed it to blend with the derivative of ᴹ✶ and assume the additional meanings “keen, sharp” (Ety/LAIK).

A noun meaning “elm-tree” developed from the root ᴹ√ (Ety/ÁLAM). An identical form appeared elsewhere in The Etymologies with its language marked “D”, perhaps for Doriathrin (Ety/LÁLAM). This word is unusual in that its final [m] did not become syllabic after a consonant, although it did for other similar words such as .

Where the diphthongs [ei] and [ou] developed at a later stage in Ilkorin, from the vocalization of [z] or of [g], these diphthongs developed into [ē] and [ou], as opposed to primitive ᴹ✶[ei] and ᴹ✶[ou] which became [ī] and [ū] respectively (PE19/25). The development is well-attested for [ou] > [au]: ᴹ✶ > kogna > coun > Ilk. (Ety/KUƷ). This rule is more speculative in the case of [ei] > [ē], but can be deduced from examples like ᴹ✶ > Ilk. (EtyAC/EZDĒ). Helge Fauskanger suggested instead that this might simply be due to the lengthening of the original [e] rather than the development of a diphthong [ei] (AL-Doriathrin/méd).

word.gloss: licking up (food or drink), gluttonous eating

ref.gloss: licking up (food or drink), gluttonous eating

word.notes: A Doriathrin noun for “gold” developed from primitive ᴹ✶, properly golden light rather than the metal (Ety/LÁWAR).

An adjective meaning “tuneful, sweet” developed from primitive ᴹ✶ (Ety/LIND, EtyAC/LIND). It is an example of how the usual Ilkorin a-affection was prevented or reverted before [nd], as suggested by Helge Fauskanger (AL-Ilkorin/lind). This word may also have had the sense “*singing” in the word “nightingale = *night singing”, from primitive ᴹ✶.

A noun for “pool” derived from the root ᴹ√ (Ety/LIN¹). Its Quenya cognate ᴹQ. suggests its primitive form was *✶linyā [linjā]. If so, it is an example of how, after final [a] was lost, the final [j] became [i] and then became [e], as suggested by Helge Fauskanger (AL-Ilkorin/line).

A Doriathrin noun for “fish” derived from primitive ᴹ✶ (Ety/LIW). It is the clearest example of how , as suggested by Helge Fauskanger (AL-Doriathrin/líw). @@@ same development in ᴱN hiw PE13/147

Conceptual Development: This word first appeared as rejected ling (EtyAC/LIW), probably reflecting Tolkien’s uncertainty on the development of [-ŋgw-] in Ilkorin.
Ilkorin name of N. , from which the Noldorin name was derived (Ety/LAM). It is a combination of “echoing” and “land”.
Ilkorin name of N. , from which the Noldorin name was derived (Ety/LAM). It is a combination of “echoing” and the plural of “mountain”.

This phonetic change is common to all Eldarin languages and is very well attested. Most likely this was a parallel change rather than a change taking place in Common Eldarin; there is evidence that it occurred later in Quenya @@@. This change is sufficiently common that it is omitted from the etymologies of Ilkorin words unless it is explicitly documented.

word.v: long vowels shortened in final syllables
word.notes: There are several clear examples of Ilkorin words that had long vowels in what would eventually become its final syllable, but the vowel is short in the Ilkorin word: ᴹ✶ > Dor. Luthien (Ety/LUK) and ᴹ✶ > Dor. (LR/188). There are also no Ilkorin polysyllables with long vowels in the final syllable. The likeliest explanation was that long vowels were shortened in final syllables. The rule also seems to apply to compounds, such as Ilk. “Wet Head” = + (Ety/MIZD).

An adjective meaning “empty” attested only as an element in the Ilkorin name (Ety/MAP). As suggested by Helge Fauskanger, it might be a combination of Dor. and the adjective suffix , but if so it is unclear where the medial g came from (AL-Ilkorin/Mablosgen). Alternately, perhaps losgen is the general Ilkorin adjective for “empty” and lost is a variant used only in the Doriathrin dialect.

A Doriathrin adjective meaning “empty” attested only as an element in the name Dor. (Ety/KAB). Its Quenya cognate suggests a primitive form *✶lustā, with the [o] developing from Ilkorin a-affection. It might be a Doriathrin-only variant of more general Ilkorin “empty”.

A Doriathrin adjective for “pale” derived from primitive ᴹ✶, a revision of the form luin that appeared in The Etymologies as published in The Lost Road (Ety/LUG², EtyAC/LUG²). The revision of [ui] >> [ū] probably reflects Tolkien’s vacillation on how primitive in Ilkorin. The earlier form of this word might an element in the name “Werewolf” (LR/134), which in earlier writings was glossed “Werewolf Pale” (LB/205). The early Noldorin word ᴱN. “pale” might be a precursor to it (PE13/149).

A Doriathrin adjective for “heavy” derived from primitive ᴹ✶ (Ety/LUG¹). It is an example of how the Ilkorin a-affection was prevented or reverted before [ŋg], as suggested by Helge Fauskanger (AL-Doriathrin/lung).

An unglossed Doriathrin word derived from the root ᴹ√ “magic, enchantment” appearing as an element in the name “Enchantress” (Ety/LUK). Since it ends in -th [θ], it probably developed from a primitive form such as *✶luktē̆, as suggested by Helge Fauskanger (AL-Doriathrin/luth). This primitive form is likely the basis for its Noldorin cognate N. “spell, charm” as well, so the Doriathrin word probably has a similar meaning. The primitive [kt] would have developed into [xθ] when double voiceless stops became spirants and this simplified to [θ] when . There was a similar development for < ᴹ✶.

An Ilkorin and Doriathrin noun for “hand” derived from primitive ᴹ✶ (Ety/MAP, EtyAC/MAP), where the voiceless stop [p] voiced to [b] after the vowel. Since its primitive form had a short [a] and its Ilkorin form a long [ā] (EtyAC/MAP), this word is an example of how in Ilkorin.
A rejected Ilkorin name from The Etymologies from the 1930s, possibly a variation of Ilk. (EtyAC/LUY). It seems to be a combination of “hand” and the rejected form luin of “pale”.
A noun for “dough” derived from primitive ᴹ✶ (Ety/MASAG), where the primitive , as suggested by Helge Fauskanger (AL-Ilkorin/maig).

An adjective meaning “soft, pliant” derived from primitive ᴹ✶ (EtyAC/MASAG). It had essentially the same development as the noun “dough” (from ᴹ✶), because in both cases the primitive final vowel vanished without further effect.

As indicated in the Comparative Tables, medial [j] (= “y”) became [i] in Ilkorin (PE19/23). There are no clear examples of this development in The Etymologies, though there are several examples where final [j] became [i]. Helge Fauskanger suggested that the primitive form of “bright” might be *✶galjānā (AL-Ilkorin/gelion); if so, it would be an example of this medial development.

word.v: medial velars with following [j] became dentals
word.notes: According to the sound changes in the Comparative Tables, it seems that medial labialized velars became non-labialized dentals in Ilkorin: see below (PE19/23). There are no attested examples of this development in The Etymologies, though compare and where this change seems to have occurred initially. In general the [j] was lost after dentalization, but after primitive [kʰ] > [x] > [θ], the [j] became [i] (and then the [θ] became [ð]).

word.v: medial voiceless spirants voiced after vowels
word.notes:
This rule is implied by the Comparative Tables, where medial aspirates became voiced spirants (PE19/23). Since at first , this means those medial voiceless spirant must later have become voiced. The examples in The Etymologies indicate this change occurred medially after vowels (Dor. ), but not after consonants (Ilk. ) or finally (Ilk. ).

In the Comparative Tables, the medial development for the aspirate [kʰ] is somewhat obscure, given as “kh > h > -” (PE19/23). Since medial [h] did not disappear when it developed from khw, I think the likeliest explanation is that the velar [x] that developed from [kʰ] first voiced to [ɣ], after which the .

There are numerous examples of final unvoiced spirants in Ilkorin, such as < ᴹ✶. This implies that the medial voicing occurred after primitive final vowels vanished. It cannot be the case that final spirants later lost their voicing, since there are also examples of final voiced spirants, such as < ᴹ✶.

There are a number of names that are possible counter-examples to this rule: Ilk. , Dor. , Dor. and Ilk. . Most of these can be explained as later compounds, but the last is given an explicit primitive form ᴹ✶ [ndanitʰārō] and cognates in other languages (LR/188). This name does not appear in The Etymologies, so perhaps Tolkien was thinking of another phonetic scenario when this name was coined.

Helge Fauskanger (writing before the Comparative Tables were published) suggested an alternate theory: that the medial voicing did not occur between vowels, but only before certain consonants (AL-Doriathrin/hedhu). The two clear examples of this change showed this development only before [w] and [m], so perhaps in between writing the Comparative Tables and The Etymologies, Tolkien decided that the medial voicing only occurred before labials or some similar scenario.

word.v: medial voiceless stops, nasals and [ɣ] became [s] before [s]
word.notes: For voiceless stops, this rule can be deduced from examples in The Etymologies: ᴹ✶ > Ilk. (Ety/TUP), ᴹ✶ > Ilk. (Ety/TAK) and ᴹ√ > [natsē >] Dor. (Ety/NAT), the last example implied by its cognate ᴹQ. . For the nasals and [ɣ], the rule is described in Tolkien’s late notes on the development of Beleriandic [Ilkorin] ʒ and ñ, where he stated that “medial ñs > ns > ss; ʒs > ss” (PE18/104), though there are no attested examples of these changes. The development of [ms] is unclear, but it may have become [ss] as well.

word.v: medial voiceless stops were voiced after nasals
word.notes: This rule is a counterpart to the rule that . There are two examples of this rule: ᴹ✶ > Dor. (Ety/KWET) and ᴹ✶ > Ilk. (Ety/TAK). There are no examples of this rule for [mp], but it may also have applied to this combination. Helge Fauskanger noted these developments in his analysis, and hypothesized that it might apply to Ilk. as well (AL-Doriathrin/cwindor; AL-Ilkorin/tangol, tingla-). It seems that this change did not occur finally or in later compounds: Ilk. or Ilk. .

A Doriathrin noun for “moisture” derived from primitive ᴹ✶ (Ety/MIZD). The [i] lengthened due to the vocalization of [z] before voiced stops, as suggested by Helge Fauskanger (AL-Doriathrin/míd). According to Carl Hostetter and Patrick Wynne, this form was originally unglossed and may have been initially intended to mean “fine rain” like its Quenya cognate ᴹQ. (EtyAC/MIZD, VTE/45).
A word for “jewel” attested only in compounds, probably of the same derivation and meaning as its Noldorin cognate N. .
A rejected and hard-to-analyze Ilkorin name for the Silmarils appearing in The Etymologies from the 1930s, revised to N. (EtyAC/MIR). It seems to contain “jewel”.
A noun for “night” derived from primitive ᴹ✶ (EtyAC/MOR), where the primitive [ǭ] became [ō].

A Doriathrin noun for “sorcery”, written as mor(n)gul indicating the loss of an earlier n (Ety/ÑGOL). The elements of this word seem to be a combination of derivatives of the roots ᴹ√ and ᴹ√. The u in the final element -gul is problematic phonetically, as it is in the similar word . Tolkien first wrote this word as morgol (EtyAC/ÑGOL), probably reflecting this phonetic uncertainty. As with , Tolkien may have resolved this uncertainty by deciding this word was Noldorin, since N. appears in a marginal note in The Etymologies (EtyAC/ÑGOL).

A Doriathrin noun for “pool”, derived from root ᴹ√ (Ety/MBOTH). Its Quenya cognate ᴹQ. suggests a primitive form of *✶mbottʰō. As pointed out by Helge Fauskanger (AL-Doriathrin/moth), the primitive [mb-] might be expected to have become [b-], since in Ilkorin, as for example Ilk. < MBIRÍL.

see-further.v: initial nasals usually vanished before stops

word.notes: A Doriathrin adjective meaning “secret, veiled” derived from root ᴹ√ (Ety/MUY), apparently a combination of “vagueness” and the adjective-suffix -in.

The Ilkorin noun for “nightingale”, appearing as both murilind and myrilind (Ety/MOR, TIN). Its Quenya cognate ᴹQ. indicates a primitive form of *✶morilindē, further supported by the rejected Ilkorin form morilind (EtyAC/MOR). This would have produced murilind according to the rules of Ilkorin i-affection. The variant form myrilind hints at a different (dialectical?) phonetic development, as pointed out by Helge Fauskanger (AL-Ilkorin/murilind). See the entry on i-affection for further discussion.
A Doriathrin noun meaning “field, valley” (Ety/NAD), also appearing as nan and described as “land at foot of hill with many streams” (EtyAC/NAD).

ref.gloss: land at foot of hill with many streams

word.notes: An Ilkorin place name appearing in The Etymologies from the 1930s, likely a combination of “valley” and the name (Ety/DAY).
A Doriathrin noun for “web” (Ety/NAT). Its Quenya cognate ᴹQ. indicates a primitive form *✶natsē, where the [ts] became [ss] because medial voiceless stops became [s] before [s] in Ilkorin.

A Doriathrin word for “Dwarf” derived from the root ᴹ√NAUK- or (Ety/NAUK). Tolkien said that it was a diminutive form, not a direct cognate of ᴹQ. or N. . It may be derived from a primitive form such as *✶naukle, as suggested by Helge Fauskanger (AL-Doriathrin/naugol), though there isn’t enough evidence to determine the original final vowel, since primitive final vowels vanished in Ilkorin. The final -ol appeared because [o] developed between a consonant and final [l] in Ilkorin.

Its form naugla appears as an element in Dor. “Necklace of the Dwarves” (Ety/NAUK).

A Doriathrin noun meaning “face” derived from the root ᴹ√ (Ety/NIB). The vowel change suggests a primitive form *✶niba, where the [i] became [e] because of Ilkorin a-affection. If this is the case, it is not a direct cognate of N. “front, face”.

The Doriathrin number “three” attested only as an element in the word “beech” = “three trunks” (Ety/NEL). Its cognates ᴹQ. and N. indicates a primitive form *✶neledē, which would have become Ilk. neld due to the Ilkorin syncope, as suggested by Helge Fauskanger (AL-Doriathrin/neldor).

A Doriathrin adjective for “wise, magical” derived from the root ᴹ√ (Ety/ÑGOL, THIN). In an earlier version of this entry, the forms were ngûl and gûl, but these were rejected (EtyAC/ÑGOL). It may be that Tolkien was considering making this another case where long [ō] became [ū] in Ilkorin, but he rejected the idea. In the entry for ÑGOL in The Etymologies, it appeared as both ngôl and gôl; the first of seems to be a variant of the usual rule that initial [ŋg] became [g] in Ilkorin.

see-further.v: initial nasals usually vanished before stops

word.gloss: one of the wise folk, Gnome
word.notes: A Doriathrin name for the ᴹQ. from the same primitive root ᴹ√ÑGÓLOD (Ety/ÑGOLOD). In the entry for ÑGOLOD in The Etymologies, it appeared as (n)gold, indicating a variation of the usual rule that initial [ŋg] became [g] in Ilkorin. The second [o] of the primitive form was lost due to the Ilkorin syncope. Its genitive form golda also appeared as an element in the name “*Noldo-jewel” = Silmaril.

see-further.v: initial nasals usually vanished before stops

ref.gloss: one of the wise folk, Gnome

word.gloss: one of the wise folk, Gnome

word.notes: A Doriathrin noun for “magic, lore” from the primitive root ᴹ√ (Ety/ÑGOL), most likely from the primitive form *✶ŋgolwe based on its Quenya cognate ᴹQ. . In the entry for ÑGOL in The Etymologies, it appeared as (n)golo, indicating a variation of the usual rule that initial [ŋg] became [g] in Ilkorin. After its final vowel was lost, the final [w] became [u], which then became [o], the only Doriathrin example of this second change.

see-further.v: initial nasals usually vanished before stops

word.notes: A Doriathrin noun for “horror” derived from the root ᴹ√ÑGÓROTH (Ety/ÑGOROTH). Its Noldorin cognate N. indicates a primitive form *✶ŋgorotʰo, where the second o was lost due to the Ilkorin syncope. Ordinarily, an initial ng- became g- in Ilkorin, as noted by Helge Fauskanger (AL-Doriathrin/ngorth), and ngorth seems to be a variation on this rule.

see-further.v: initial nasals usually vanished before stops

word.notes: A Doriathrin adjective meaning “horrible”, a combination of “horror” with the adjective suffix -in (Ety/ÑGOROTH).

A Doriathrin word meaning “forward” or “west”, derived from the root ᴹ√ (Ety/NIB). It could have developed from primitive forms like *✶nibon or *✶nibn(ǝ), with -on developing in the second example because [o] developed between a consonant and a final [n] in Ilkorin. As noted by Helge Fauskanger (AL-Doriathrin/nivon), the sense “west” probably developed from the meaning “forward” because the Elves thought of themselves as facing West when marking directions.
A Doriathrin noun for “nose” derived from ᴹ✶ (Ety/LIW). It is likely an example of how , especially if the [e] first became [i] before the [ŋg], as suggested by Helge Fauskanger (AL-Doriathrin/nîw).
Of the few grammatical inflections for Ilkorin attested in The Etymologies, almost all of them have to do with nouns.

An adjective meaning “hideous, horrible” derived from the root ᴹ√ (Ety/ÚLUG). Its Telerin cognate ᴹT. indicates a primitive form *✶ulgā, so that in the Ilkorin word the short [u] became [o] preceding the final [a] before that final vowel vanished.
Apparently a masculine suffix attested in the name .

A noun for “blood” derived from the root ᴹ√ (Ety/YAR). Its cognates ᴹQ. and N. indicates a primitive form *✶yār(ǝ) [jārǝ], where the vowel changed to [o] because of Ilkorin a-affection. Helge Fauskanger suggested instead that the primitive form was *✶yara because of the Quenya stem form yar-, with a lengthening of the vowel in the primitive monosyllabic form (AL-Ilkorin/ôr) @@@ examine further.

A Doriathrin noun for “tree” derived from the root ᴹ√ÓR-NI or ᴹ√ÓRON (Ety/ÓR-NI, EtyAC/NEL). According Tolkien, it was “in Doriath used especially of beech, but as a suffix [it was] used of any tree of any size” (Ety/ÓR-NI). The root ᴹ√ÓR-NI in The Etymologies suggests a primitive form of ᴹ✶ornĭ, but elsewhere Tolkien indicated the primitive form was ᴹ✶ornē (e.g. on SD/302). Both primitive forms would have produced Ilk. orn, as noted by Helge Fauskanger (AL-Doriathrin/orn).

A Doriathrin noun for “mountain” derived from the root ᴹ√ÓROT (Ety/ÓROT). Its Old Noldorin cognate ON. suggests a primitive form *✶orotō, where the second [o] was lost due to the Ilkorin syncope [orto]. Later the [t] became [θ] (“th”) because in Ilkorin. Both these developments were noted by Helge Fauskanger (AL-Doriathrin/orth). This word has two distinct plural forms attested: Dor. orthin (Ety/ÓROT) and Ilk. urthin (EtyAC/WATH); this could represent distinct rules for the formation of in the two dialects.

Apparently an abstract noun suffix appearing in the words and , perhaps of the same origin as the abstract endings ᴹQ. and N. , though Helge Fauskanger suggested instead that it is related to the locative suffix ᴹQ. (AL-Ilkorin/thalos).
A noun for “war” derived from primitive ᴹ✶ (Ety/OKTĀ). It is a good example of how in Ilkorin, in this case [kt] > [xθ] (or [θθ]) > [θ].

There are quite a few attested plurals in The Etymologies for both Doriathrin and Ilkorin nouns. From these we can deduce a number of features for the Ilkorin and Doriathrin plurals.

The plural suffix : With two exceptions (see below), all the attested plurals in both Doriathrin and Ilkorin use the suffix -in. This seems to be the basic mechanism of plural formation for nouns. It is likely this suffix was inspired by the Gnomish plural suffix .

The i-affection of [a] and [o]: The plurals of Ilkorin nouns containing short vowels [a] and [o] have these vowels shift to [e] and [u] according to the normal rules of Ilkorin i-affection. The clearest examples of this change are Ilk. → pl. lelmin (Ety/ÁLAM) and Ilk. → pl. thurnin (Ety/THOR). This change did not occur for long vowels, such as Ilk. → pl. tórin (Ety/BAL); long [ā] did not normally occur in Ilkorin.

This i-affection does not seem to occur for plurals in the Doriathrin dialect: Dor. roth → pl. rodhin (Ety/ROD) and Dor. than → gen. pl. thanion (LR/405). In fact, there is one noun that has plurals in both Ilkorin and Doriathrin, with Ilk. pl. urthin (EtyAC/WATH) versus Dor. pl. orthin (Ety/ÓROT). This lack of i-affection seems only to be true of the noun plural and not the general phonological history of Doriathrin: consider Dor. and Dor. , in which an older [a] became [e] before an [i].

Syncope of vowels in final syllables: In polysyllabic Ilkorin nouns, the vowel in the final syllable is lost when the plural suffix is added: Ilk. → pl. edrin (Ety/ATA) and Ilk. → pl. telmin (Ety/TAL). The i-affection of [a] and [o] noted above also applied in these cases. This change did not occur when the result would be an invalid cluster of vowels: Ilk. → pl. Balthorin (Ety/BAL), but could occur where the cluster was acceptable: Ilk. → pl. genglin (Ety/ÑGAN).

Note that there are no attested examples of plurals for polysyllabic Doriathrin nouns, so it is unclear whether this rule would apply to that dialect. However, based on the syncope in the genitive inflection Dor. → naugla (Ety/NAUK), it seems likely that this rule would apply to Doriathrin as well.

Preservation of stem forms: In some nouns, older stem forms were preserved in the plural. For example, in Doriathrin a , such as ᴹ✶roda > [roð >] Dor. roth (Ety/ROD, EtyAC/ROD). The older form [roð] is preserved in its plural form rodhin. Similarly, the word Dor. “holly-tree” still uses its simpler form “holly” in its plurals: Dor. pl. regin and gen. pl. region (Ety/ERÉK).

Plural using only i-affection: There is one Ilkorin plural produced exclusively by i-affection without the suffix -in: Ilk. → pl. tel (Ety/TAL). Without further examples, however, it is unclear when this variant plural would or would not occur.

A Doriathrin word for “east”, derived from the root ᴹ√ “back, return” (Ety/RAD). It could have developed from primitive forms like *✶radon or *✶radn(ǝ), with -on developing in the second example because [o] developed between a consonant and a final [n] in Ilkorin. As noted by Helge Fauskanger (AL-Doriathrin/radhon), the sense “east” probably developed from the meaning “back” because the Elves thought of themselves as facing West when marking directions, so that East was behind them.
A Doriathrin place name appearing in The Etymologies from the 1930s, a combination of “east” and “border” (Ety/RAD, RĪ).

A word meaning “flow, course of river” derived from the root ᴹ√ (Ety/RAT). It probably developed from an nasal-infixed variant of the root such *✶ranta, as suggested by Helge Fauskanger (AL-Ilkorin/rant).

A Doriathrin noun for “holly” attested only in the plural forms regin and region (Ety/ERÉK). It also appeared as an element in the word “holly-tree”. It seems that the latter word replaced reg in the singular, and the original survived only in the plurals, as suggested by Helge Fauskanger (AL-Doriathrin/regorn).
A Doriathrin noun meaning “holly-tree”, a combination of (archaic?) “holly” and “tree” (Ety/ERÉK, ÓR-NI).
A Doriathrin variation of appearing in The Etymologies from the 1930s (Ety/ÉREK). It was translated “Hollin” and appears to be the genitive plural of Ilk. “holly-tree”.
word.related: is an earlier form given the same translation as

word.notes: A noun meaning “a cut” derived from the root ᴹ√ (Ety/RIS²). Its Quenya cognate ᴹQ. suggests a primitive form *✶ristā, where the [i] became [e] due to Ilkorin a-affection, as noted by Helge Fauskanger (AL-Ilkorin/rest).
A Doriathrin noun for “precipice” derived from primitive ᴹ✶ (EtyAC/KHARÁS), an example of how in Ilkorin.
A Doriathrin noun meaning “edge, hem, border” derived from the root ᴹ√RĪ (Ety/RĪ). Its Quenya cognate ᴹQ. suggests a primitive form *✶rīmā, where the primitive final vowel vanished in Ilkorin.

A Doriathrin noun meaning “cold pool or lake (in mountains)” derived from the root ᴹ√ (Ety/RINGI). Its Quenya cognate ᴹQ. suggests a primitive form *✶riñgwi [riŋgwi]. This is problematic, since , as with Dor. < ᴹ✶liñ(g)wi. It is possible, though, that this word developed directly from the root form *✶riñgi [riŋgi], as suggested by Helge Fauskanger (AL-Doriathrin/ring).
A noun meaning “domed roof” derived from a nasal-infixed form of the root ᴹ√ “roof, cave” (Ety/ROD).
A Doriathrin noun meaning “plain, wide land between mountains” derived from the root ᴹ√ (Ety/ROS²).

A Doriathrin noun for “cave”, also appearing as roth, derived from primitive ᴹ✶ or ᴹ✶roda (Ety/ROD, EtyAC/ROD). The [d] spirantilized to [ð] (“dh”) as usual, then after the final vowel was lost the as suggested by Helge Fauskanger (AL-Doriathrin/roth). The original sound [ð] is preserved in the plural rodhin.
A noun for “grass” derived from the root ᴹ√ (Ety/SALÁK). It is a good example of how in Ilkorin.

A noun meaning “drinking-vessel” derived from primitive ᴹ✶ (Ety/SUK). This word went through a number of phonetic changes:

  • the [k] became [g] before the nasal [m]
  • the [u] shifted to [o] before the final [a]
  • the [g] vocalized to [u] before the nasal [m] producing the diphthong [ou]
  • the resulting diphthong [ou] became [au]

Helge Fauskanger originally suggested these developments (AL-Ilkorin/saum).

word.v: second unstressed short vowel of same quality lost
word.notes:
Like the Quenya syncope, a short vowel of the same quality as the preceding syllable was lost in Ilkorin, for example: ᴹ✶ > Dor. (EtyAC/KWEN(ED)) or ᴹ✶thóron[ē] > Ilk. (Ety/THOR). There is one example indicating that this change could occur even when the second primitive vowel was stressed: ᴹ✶salák-(wē) > Ilk. (Ety/SALÁK). In this case, though, it is likely that the stress shifted to the initial syllable before the vowel was lost.

There are a couple of counter-examples to this rule. First, the syncope did not occur when the result would be a cluster of three consonants: ᴹ✶ > Ilk. (Ety/TUB), although it seems that if the third consonant was the semi-vowel [w], the syncope could still occur (see salch above). Second, it seems that the syncope did not occur when the second vowel was in the final syllable: ᴹ✶bóron- > Ilk. (Ety/BOR); this exception may apply to Ilk. as well (Ety/AM¹). In these last two examples, the syncope did apply to the plurals: burnin and emnin, where the lost vowel would no longer be in the last syllable.

It seems likely that the syncope occurred before , since ᴹ✶gálad[ā] > Ilk. (Ety/GALAD) and ᴹ✶ñgólod[ō] > Ilk. (Ety/ÑGOLOD) rather than **galdh [galð] or **goldh [golð]. However, it is possible the syncope occurred afterwards, and voiced spirants were re-stopped in these positions.

These developments mirror the well-known changes of Noldorin, often called the i-affection or i-umlaut. In Ilkorin, the rule seems to be that when a short [a] or [o] appeared before another syllable containing [i], these vowels shifted to [e] or [u] respectively. One clear example of this change is ᴹ✶ > Dor. (LR/188). This rule is also important to the formation of in Ilkorin, since the plural suffix was ; consider → (plural) lelmin (Ety/ÁLAM) and → (plural) thurnin (Ety/THOR).

Like the Noldorin rule, it appears that this sound change did not occur for long vowels: consider “queen” (Ety/TĀ), “king” → (plural) tôrin (Ety/BAL) and “pine” → (genitive plural) thonion (Ety/THŌN). It is unclear whether the Ilkorin i-affection carried through to syllables further forward in the word, as was the case for Noldorin.

Special cases: One peculiar example is Ilk. “nightingale”, which appears beside the form murilind (Ety/MOR, TIN). The form murilind seems to have been produced by regular i-affection from primitive *✶morilind(e), but development of [y] is difficult to explain. Since the initial element of the primitive form was ᴹ✶, perhaps the [o] was more fronted, resulting in i-affection into [y] instead of [u]. As further evidence of this, the word was adapted into Noldorin as the front-vowel [œ]: mœrilind > (Ety/TIN, EtyAC/TIN). Since this is the only instance of the vowel [y] appearing in Ilkorin, it is hard to figure out what Tolkien intended here.

An i-affection of [e] to [i] also seems logical when comparing to the sound changes of Noldorin, but there is little evidence of such a change. The only attested example is the (hypothetical) name from the root ᴹ√ (Ety/GYEL), which may have undergone this change when developing from the (even more speculative) primitive form *Gyelion. However, the change did not occur in the plural forms regin from (Ety/ERÉK) or Eldin from (Ety/ELED), so it is probably better to assume Dilion is a special case, perhaps a side effect of the change of initial [gj-] to [d-].

These developments mirror the well-known changes of Noldorin, often called the a-affection or a-umlaut. Where an [i] or [u] appeared in a syllable before a primitive final [a] (including a-stem verbs), these vowels shift to [e] and [o] respectively. Since the final [a] usually disappeared (except in a-stem verbs), this sound shift can give a clue to the more primitive forms of words. Some clear examples of this change are ᴹ✶rista > Ilk. (Ety/RIS²) and ᴹ✶ > Ilk. (Ety/TUL).

In Ilkorin, this sound change seems to be prevented or reverted in some cases: see the rule that for further discussion. Variations in the adjective suffix vs. -in (from ᴹ✶-inā) may also indicate some uncertainty on Tolkien’s part on the exact functioning of this rule.

In Ilkorin, nearly all original primitive final vowels vanished, which was also the rule in Noldorin. First all , then the remaining short final vowels vanished. Any Ilkorin words ending in vowels were the result of some other process, such as final [j], [w] becoming [i], [u] (after which they became [e], [o] in most cases). The loss of final vowels in Ilkorin is very well attested in The Etymologies; see below for examples.

Final [-o] became [-a] after [g] and [ɣ]: One possible counter-example to this rule is ᴹ✶ > Ilk. (Ety/MORÓK). Here the final [-go] seems to have developed into [-ga] instead losing its final vowel, as suggested by Helge Fauskanger (AL-Ilkorin/broga). Another example (also suggested by Helge Fauskanger, AL-Ilkorin/-a) is the genitive suffix , which might have developed from primitive ᴹ✶ [ɣō]; this example hints that this development occurred after [ɣ] as well. A third possible example is “daddy” (from ?✶attō), again suggested by Helge Fauskanger (AL-Ilkorin/adda). I find this last example less compelling, however, since this child’s word may simply be a late invention rather than a derivation from a primitive form. The theory presented here assumes that [-o] became [-a] after [g] and [ɣ] but not otherwise.

Final [-u] sometimes was preserved? Another possible preservation of a final vowel might be Ilk. , whose Quenya cognate ᴹQ. “a male” implies the survival of a primitive final [-u] (Ety/ƷAN). One possible explanation is that it was not a true cognate, but instead developed from a primitive adjective [ɣanwā], and thus had its final [u] develop from the [w], as suggested by Helge Fauskanger (AL-Doriathrin/ganu). The Noldorin development ᴹ√ > ON. > N. seems to contradict this scenario however, so perhaps the final -u was preserved by comparing the noun and adjective forms in both Ilkorin and Noldorin.

There are no clear examples of final [-u] being lost in Ilkorin. The only possible example is ᴹ✶ [?urku] > (Ety/ÓROK), but in this case the short final [u] would have become [o] primitively, as indicated by its cognates ON. and ᴹQ. .

before.v: medial voiceless spirants voiced after vowels

word.v: short vowels sometimes lengthened in monosyllables
word.notes: There are a few examples where a primitive short vowel became long in Ilkorin monosyllables, such as ᴹ✶ > Ilk. (Ety/MAP, EtyAC/MAP) and ᴹ✶ > Dor. (EtyAC/NDOR). There was a similar development in Noldorin, but unlike Noldorin, there are numerous Ilkorin monosyllables where this change did not occur, such as , and . There does not seem to be a clear pattern to the few monosyllables where the vowel did lengthen.

An adjective meaning “firm, stiff, solid” derived from the root ᴹ√ (Ety/TAK). Since it ends with “ch” [x] instead of “g”, most likely its primitive form was *✶takka, since in Ilkorin. Its middle vowel must have been a short [a], otherwise the long [ā] would have become [ō]. Therefore, this word is an example of how in Ilkorin. Both these phonetic developments were noted by Helge Fauskanger in his study of Ilkorin (AL-Ilkoring/tâch).

A verb meaning “to fix, construct, make” derived from the root ᴹ√, attested only its 3rd singular present tense form taga “he fixes, constructs, makes” (Ety/TAK). The [k] became [g] after a vowel as usual.
An adjective meaning “steep, tall, deep” derived from primitive ᴹ✶ (Ety/AYAK, EtyAC/TĀ). The [k] became [g] after a vowel as usual.
A noun for “foot” derived from the ᴹ√ (Ety/TAL). It is unusual in that its plural form tel involved Ilkorin i-affection but not the suffix , as noted by Helge Fauskanger (AL-Ilkorin/tal).

A noun meaning “ground, floor” derived from the root ᴹ√ (Ety/TALAM). Most likely it developed from primitive *✶talama, first losing the second [a] due to the Ilkorin syncope and the final [a] when , after which the resulting final [m] became syllabic and developed into [um]. These developments were suggested by Helge Fauskanger (AL-Ilkorin/talum).

A noun meaning “pin, brooch” derived from primitive ᴹ✶ [taŋkla] (Ety/TAK). First the [k] became [g] after the nasal [ŋ] and then final [l] became syllabic and developed into [ol]. These developments were suggested by Helge Fauskanger (AL-Ilkorin/tangol).
An adjective meaning “tough, stiff” derived from primitive ᴹ✶ after primitive final vowels vanished (Ety/TÁRAG).
A noun for “pin” derived from primitive ᴹ✶ (Ety/TAK), where the [ks] became [ss] because medial voiceless stops became [s] before [s] in Ilkorin.

A noun meaning “holder, socket, hasp, clasp, staple” developed from the primitive form ᴹ✶ (Ety/KUƷ). Most likely its development was similar to that of : first the [k] became [g] before the nasal, then the [g] vocalized to [u] before the [m] and finally the diphthong [ou] became [au].
A noun meaning “wood (place and material), forest” derived from primitive ᴹ✶ after primitive final vowels vanished (Ety/TÁWAR).

A noun for “silver” derived from the root ᴹ✶KYÉLEP (Ety/KYELEP), most likely from a primitive form *✶kyelepē [kjelepē]. In Ilkorin, the initial [t] developed from [kj] because , the middle [e] vanished due to the Ilkorin syncope, and the [p] became [f] because voiceless stops became spirants after liquids (like [l]). These developments were all suggested by Helge Fauskanger (AL-Ilkorin/telf).

A noun meaning “close, end, last part” derived from the root ᴹ√ (EtyAC/TELES). Its Quenya cognates ᴹQ. and ᴹQ. (< ᴹ✶) suggest a primitive form of *✶telesē. The middle [e] would have vanished due to the Ilkorin syncope, after which apparently the , though this is the only example of this change.

A noun meaning “carpenter, wright, builder” derived from primitive ᴹ✶ (Ety/STAB). The initial [s] spirantalized the following [t] to [θ] (“th”), while the [b] spirantalized to [v] after a vowel, and [n] became syllabic, developing into [-on] after it became final. These developments were all suggested by Helge Fauskanger (AL-Ilkorin/thavon).
A shorter Ilkorin name for Ilk. appearing in The Etymologies from the 1930s (Ety/THIN). It is simply “grey” used as a name.
An adjective for “grey” derived from primitive ᴹ✶ (Ety/THIN) because primitive final vowels vanished in Ilkorin.

A noun for “pine-tree” derived from the root ᴹ√, also appearing in its genitive plural form thonion “of pines” (Ety/THŌN, EtyAC/THŌN). Helge Fauskanger suggested that it developed from primitive *✶thon- with a short ŏ because the [ō] did not become [ū] before the nasal (AL-Ilkorin/thôn), and only later did the short vowel lengthen in the monosyllable. I think that Mr. Fauskanger may have over-generalized this rule, however, since the other examples of [ō] becoming [ū] occur only before [m] and the change may not have applied to nasals in general. If this is the case, this word could have developed from primitive *✶thōn-. There is not enough evidence to say for certain either way.

Conceptual Development: In notes elsewhere this word was given the form Dor. than with genitive plural form thanion (LR/405), probably associated with the earlier name Dorthanion versus later (LR/145). It is also possible these are Doriathrin and Ilkorin variations of the same word.

A noun for “eagle” derived from the root ᴹ√THÓRON (Ety/THOR). Its cognates ᴹQ. and N. suggest a primitive form *✶thoronē, where the middle [o] was lost due to the Ilkorin syncope. Its plural form is not thurin as printed in The Lost Road, but is actually thurnin matching its singular (EtyAC/THOR), as predicted by Helge Fauskanger (AL-Ilkorin/thorn).
Ilkorin name for N. appearing in The Etymologies from the 1930s, translated “King of Eagles” (Ety/THOR). It is a combination of “eagle” and “king”.

An adjective meaning “stiff, hard” derived from primitive ᴹ✶ (Ety/STARAN). First the unstressed vowel in the first syllable vanished to produce the favored combination [tr], after which the initial [s] spirantalized the following [t] to [θ] (“th”), while the long [ā] became [ō]. All these developments were suggested by Helge Fauskanger (AL-Ilkorin/thrôn).

A noun meaning “(starry) twilight, starlight”, a combination of “star” and “twilight” (Ety/DOMO, TIN), also appearing in its genitive form tinduma (Ety/THIN). Either the compound preserved the original [n] from tim < ᴹ✶, or the [n] reformed by assimilation to the [d].

A verb meaning “to sparkle” derived from the root ᴹ√ (Ety/TIN), most likely from a primitive verb *✶tinglā. If so, it is an example of how the Ilkorin a-affection was prevented or reverted before [ŋg]. This development was pointed out by Helge Fauskanger, though he suggested the primitive verb was *✶tintilā, a cognate Q. , with a medial development of [-nt(i)l-] > [-ngl-] (AL-Ilkorin/tingla-).
An adjective meaning “thick, fat” derived from primitive ᴹ✶ (Ety/TIW), where the primitive [iu] became [io] and the [k] voiced to [g] after the vowel, as was usual in Ilkorin.

A verb for “to bring” derived from the root ᴹ√, attested only in its 3rd-singular present form toga “he brings” (Ety/TUK). Here the short [u] became [o] before the final [a] and the [k] voiced to [g] after the vowel, as suggested by Helge Fauskanger (AL-Ilkorin/toga). The base form might be tug-.

A verb for “to fetch” derived from primitive ᴹ✶, attested only in its 3rd-singular present form tolda “he fetches” (Ety/TUK). Here the short [u] became [o] before the final [a]. The change of [lt] to [ld] is harder to explain, since ordinarily voiceless stops became spirants after liquids in Ilkorin, as noted by Helge Fauskanger (AL-Ilkorin/tolda).

A noun for “king” derived from primitive ᴹ✶, also appearing in its plural form tórin (Ety/TĀ, BAL). Tolkien said that it was “only used of the legitimate kings of whole tribes”, though apparently it also survived in compounds like “King of Eagles” (Ety/THOR) and “Vala-king” (Ety/BAL). It is an example of how [ā] became [ō] in Ilkorin, as noted by Helge Fauskanger (AL-Ilkorin/tôr).
A noun for “queen”, a combination of “king” with the feminine suffix , though according to Tolkien it was used only as a title for Melian (Ety/TĀ).
A title for appearing in The Etymologies from the 1930s, a combination of “king” with his name (Ety/TĀ, Ety/THIN).
A variant form of Ilk. , a combination of “king” and the genitive plural of “eagle” (Ety/THOR).
A title for appearing in The Etymologies from the 1930s, a combination of “king” and the genitive of “starry twilight” (Ety/THIN, TIN).

An adjective meaning “lowlying, deep, low” derived from primitive ᴹ✶ (Ety/STAB). The short [u] became [o] before the final [a], while the [b] spirantalized to [v] after a vowel, with the [n] becoming syllabic and developing into [-on] after it became final. These developments were all suggested by Helge Fauskanger (AL-Ilkorin/tovon).

An adjective meaning “fine, slender” derived from primitive ᴹ✶ (Ety/TER), where the unstressed vowel in the first syllable vanished to produce the favored combination [tr] as suggested by Helge Fauskanger (AL-Ilkorin/trêw).

A noun for “shield” derived from primitive ᴹ✶ (Ety/TER), where the unstressed vowel in the first syllable vanished to produce the favored combination [tr], and later the [mb] simplified to [m] when this cluster became final.

A noun meaning “muscle, sinew; vigour, physical strength” derived from primitive ᴹ✶ with an attested intermediate form tūgh [tūɣ] (Ety/TUG). It is a good example of how [g] spirantalized to [ɣ] (“gh”) after a vowel, and the resulting voiced velar spirant , as suggested by Helge Fauskanger (AL-Ilkorin/tû).
An adjective for “tall” derived from primitive ᴹ✶ (Ety/TUN). It is an example of how the Ilkorin a-affection was prevented or reverted before [nd], as suggested by Helge Fauskanger (AL-Ilkorin/tund).

An adjective for “taut, tight” derived from primitive ᴹ✶, meaning “resonant” when referring to strings (Ety/TUG). It is an example of how the Ilkorin a-affection was prevented or reverted before [ŋg], as suggested by Helge Fauskanger (AL-Ilkorin/tung).
A noun for “thatch” derived from primitive ᴹ✶ (Ety/TUP), where the [ps] became [ss] because medial voiceless stops became [s] before [s] in Ilkorin.
Ilkorin name for ᴹQ. appearing in The Etymologies from the 1930s, a derivative of the same primitive form ᴹ✶ (Ety/TUB).

A noun meaning “monster, deformed and hideous creature” derived from primitive ᴹ✶ (Ety/ÚLUG). Here the after other vowels and consonants were lost. This is also the only attested example of how , as noted by Helge Fauskanger (AL-Ilkorin/ulion).

A Doriathrin noun meaning “large pool”, apparently an elaboration of “pool” (Ety/MBOTH). Either the u- is some kind of prefix, perhaps an intensifier, or the initial [m] of the root became syllabic, both as suggested by Helge Fauskanger (AL-Ilkorin/umboth).

Conceptual Development: Tolkien seems to have coined this word to explain “Twilight Meres”, a remnant of earlier G. “Pools of Twilight”. The meaning of the Ilkorin elements is reversed from the earlier name: ᴱN./G. meant “nightfall” or “twilight” (GL/75; PE13/155); see that entry for discussion. In later writings, Tolkien replaced this name with S. “Meres of Twilight”.

A word appearing as G. umboth or umbath “nightfall” in the Gnomish Lexicon of the 1910s as an elaboration of the early root ᴱ√m(b)aþ- “dusk” (GL/75). It reappeared in ᴱN. umboth “twilight” in Early Noldorin word-lists (PE13/155). In the 1910s and 20s its most notable was in the name ᴱN./G. Umboth-muilin “Pools of Twilight” or “Twilight Meres” (LT2/225; LB/214), but in the 1930s Ilkorin form of this name Umboth Muilin the meaning of the first element umboth was “large pool” (Ety/MBOTH). In Tolkien’s later writings this name became Aelin-uial.

A noun for “darkness” developed from the root ᴹ√ (Ety/UÑG), perhaps from a primitive form *✶uñglē̆ [uŋglē̆] as suggested by Helge Fauskanger (AL-Ilkorin/ungol): after the primitive final [e] was lost, the resulting final [l] would become syllabic and develop into [-ol].

An adjective meaning “black, dark, gloomy” developed from the root ᴹ√ (Ety/UÑG), perhaps from a primitive form *✶uñgrā̆ [uŋgrā̆] as suggested by Helge Fauskanger (AL-Ilkorin/ungor): after the primitive final [a] was lost, the resulting final [r] would become syllabic and develop into [-or].

word.v: unstressed initial syllables reduced to favored clusters
word.notes:
In the initial syllable of a polysyllabic word, unstressed vowels tended to vanish if the result was one of several favored consonant combinations: br-, dr-, gr- or tr-. This change also occurred with mr-, but then the : ᴹ✶ > Ilk. (Ety/MORÓK). Finally, the change could occur when the favored initial combination was preceded by another consonant, such as: ᴹ✶MBIRÍL > Ilk. (m)bril (Ety/MBIRIL) or ᴹ✶ > [strāna >] Ilk. (Ety/STARAN).

In the examples of this change, the words in question had either stress marker or a long vowel in the second syllable, indicating that the first syllable was unstressed (see below). Furthermore, there are some counter-examples where the first syllable is marked as stressed and the vowel loss does not occur: ᴹ✶bóron- > Ilk. (Ety/BOR), ᴹ✶DÓRON > Ilk. (Ety/DÓRON). Finally, in all the attested examples, the lost vowel is followed by another of the same quality.

It is possible that this change occurred with other initial combinations such as pr- or kr- that are simply missing in the small list of available Ilkorin words. It is also possible that this change occurred in Common Eldarin rather than Ilkorin, since these combinations are listed as Later Combinations in the Comparative Tables (PE19/21). These tables also list combinations involving [l], such as bl- or gl-, but there are no such attested examples in Ilkorin. It is unclear whether this is because such changes did not occur, or because such examples are simply missing from the available Ilkorin word list.

A Doriathrin noun for “goblin” developed from primitive ᴹ✶, also attested in its plural form urchin (Ety/ÓROK). The change of [k] to [x] (“ch”) after the liquid [l] was a normal Ilkorin development, but the change of [o] to [u] is harder to explain, as noted by Helge Fauskanger (AL-Doriathrin/urch). In an earlier version of the entry Tolkien wrote Dor. orch (EtyAC/ÓROK), which is the expected form. The simplest explanation is that this form actually developed from a variant primitive form *✶urku. There is a similar issue with Dan. , so perhaps this variant was used by those Eldar who did not complete the journey to Valinor.
Ilkorin name for N. appearing in The Etymologies from the 1930s, a combination of the plural of “mountain” and the genitive plural of “shade” (Ety/WATH, EtyAC/WATH).

A noun for “smoke” developed from primitive ᴹ✶ (Ety/USUK). In this example, the loss of the second [u] was probably very early, since it appears in all child languages. This word is a good example of how in Ilkorin, as noted by Helge Fauskanger (AL-Ilkorin/usc).

There are six attested Ilkorin verbs. Half of them are expressed as stem forms, such as Ilk. “to soil, stain” (Ety/WAƷ) and the other half are in what appears to be a third-person singular present formation, such as Ilk. tolda “he fetches”. It seems likely that Ilkorin had both basic verbs (derived directly from the root) and a-stem or derived verbs (root + suffix) as was the case with other Eldarin languages, but it is hard to tell since all the attested forms end with -a. Similarly, the suffix -a might be a 3rd-sg. suffix, but could also just be an endingless suffix for a-stem verbs. Without further examples, it is hard to determine anything.

In notes for the Comparative Tables, Tolkien said that “in Ilk[orin] ... voiced stops became spirantal medially” (PE19/24), a change that also appeared in the tables themselves (PE19/23). This change was also the rule in Noldorin. From the examples in The Etymologies, it is clear this change occurred consistently after vowels. Some clear examples are: ᴹ✶ > Ilk. (Ety/TUB), ᴹ✶ > Ilk. [gweð] (Ety/WED) and ᴹ✶ > tūgh [tūɣ] > Ilk. (Ety/TUG).

It seems likely that this change occurred before , since the presence of a primitive [z] in this position meant that a primitive voiced stop was preserved, for example: ᴹ✶ > Ilk. (Ety/MIZD) or ᴹ✶ > Ilk. (Ety/MASAG).

word.v: voiceless stops became spirants after liquids and voiceless stops
word.notes:
This Ilkorin phonetic rule is similar to sound changes that occurred in Old Noldorin. The clearest examples of this rule are ᴹ✶kyel(e)p[e] > Ilk. (Ety/KYELEP), ᴹ✶ > Ilk. [briθ] (Ety/BIRÍT), ᴹ✶ > Ilk. [alx] (Ety/ÁLAK), and ᴹ✶ [?urku] > Dor. [urx] (Ety/ÓROK). It is possible that the voiceless stops first became aspirates [pʰ], [tʰ] and [kʰ] and then these [f], [θ] (= “th”) and [x] (= “ch”).

In the case of pairs of stops, it seems likely that both stops developed into spirants, but this change is obscured because the resulting . In the case of [kt], it seems the development was to [xθ] and then [θ], for example: ᴹ✶ > [oxθa >] Ilk. (Ety/OKTĀ).

Based on the examples Ilk. and Ilk. , it seems that this change did not occur after nasals, unlike Old Noldorin. Another aberrant form is < ᴹ✶, where the [lt] became [ld] instead of [lθ], though there is no clear reason why this happened. Helge Fauskanger suggested that perhaps [lt] became [ld] very early, and [l] + [t] only became [lθ] in later compounds like (AL-Ilkorin/tolda).

As described in the Comparative Tables, voiceless stop were voiced medially (PE19/23), which was also the rule in Noldorin. From the examples in The Etymologies, it is clear this change occurred consistently after vowels. Some clear examples are: ᴹ✶ > Ilk. (Ety/MAP), ᴹ✶ > Ilk. (Ety/ATA) and ᴹ✶ > Ilk. (Ety/TIW). This development must have occurred after , since the voiced stops resulting from this rule did not further develop into spirants.

word.v: voiceless stops were voiced before nasals
word.notes:
In the Ilkorin phonetic developments described in The Etymologies, it appears that voiceless stops were voiced before nasals, as was also the rule in Old Noldorin. The clearest example of this change is ᴹ✶ > Dor. [aðum] (EtyAC/YAT). Here the [t] must have become [d], which then spirantalized to [ð]. It could not have remained [t], because that would have produced **adum: compare ᴹ✶ > Ilk. (Ety/ATA).

A less obvious example is ᴹ✶ > Ilk. (Ety/TAK). Here it seems that the [k] became [g], which then vocalized to [u]. The evidence in this case (as well as similar developments for Ilk. ) is not as strong, since this change could conceivably be explained by the rule that .

There are no examples of this rule for [p] > [b] (then > [v]), but it seems likely the rule would apply in this case as well.

word.notes: An early dwarf name of unknown meaning appearing in the first draft of the chapter “The Mines of Moria” in the phrase “the dwarflords of Uruktharbun” (RS/458). According to Christopher Tolkien (RS/465, note 36), the name Azanulbizâr (Dimrill-dale) was pencilled next to it, but in the next version of the chapter it was changed to (Moria), so Uruktharbun could be the precursor of either of these later names.
One of the dwarves who accompanied Bilbo from Bag-end in early Lord of the Rings drafts from the 1940s (RS/238).
